title: Zero to RHCSA on RHEL 10
description: Begin with your first AlmaLinux login and build toward independent RHEL 10 administration. Practice in a live terminal beside each reading, solve shift assignments, and test your work on a two-machine RHCSA practice exam.

modules.title: Start here: meet your AlmaLinux machines
Learn how Bash reads commands and how to find help
Work with paths, text, links and backups
Manage identities, privileges and shared files
Connect the client and server by address and name
Manage signed RPM and Flatpak software
Observe running work, logs and performance
Turn repeatable work into Bash scripts
Provision disks, logical volumes and swap
Mount local storage and deliver remote files
Follow the boot chain and recover a practice guest
Rehearse, sit the practical and review the evidence
Optional extension after exam review: containers and image mode

lessons.title: Meet Linux and install your first practice machine
lessons.body:
A coworker tells you that the reports are missing from “the server.” Before changing anything, you need to know which computer holds the reports and how to ask it a question. In this course the **server** offers files and services. The **client** requests them. Both are computers running Linux. You will work on both sides of that conversation.

Linux is the **kernel**, the part of the operating system that manages devices, memory and running programs. A **distribution** packages the kernel with utilities, software and documentation. You will practice on AlmaLinux 10.3 and prepare for the RHCSA exam based on RHEL 10. A **virtual machine** (VM) is a whole guest computer with its own operating system and disk. The physical or virtual computer running Erudior is the host.

## Open your first guest

In Erudior Desktop 0.25.3 or later, select **Open practice terminal** above this reading. In **First-time setup**, follow the instructions for your host. The desktop can fetch the verified DVD and practice kit or accept both as local files. Select **Start lab**. The first build installs a base system and takes longer than later starts. Leave the app open until the machines are ready. The shared **Client console** opens when the client starts. Give it time to boot, then press Enter for the login prompt. Expand **Console login** for the username and the password for this attempt. At a Linux text login, typing the password displays no characters. Type it once and press Enter.

The reading and the terminal share the window. Click inside the terminal before typing. Press **F6** to switch focus back to the course or return to the terminal. The **Server console** button switches guests. The shared practice shell follows you to the next reading. Practical exam lessons supply separate machines for the assessment.

If you are reading in a browser, open your own AlmaLinux VM alongside it. The **Set up and reset the AlmaLinux 10.3 lab** reference walks through the two-machine kit. A browser-only reading session also lets you predict results and answer quizzes. Return to the terminal exercises when you have a guest.

[AlmaLinux 10.3 x86_64 DVD installer](https://repo.almalinux.org/almalinux/10.3/isos/x86_64/AlmaLinux-10.3-x86_64-dvd.iso) · [AlmaLinux practice kit](https://app.erudior.com/downloads/Erudior-AlmaLinux-10.3-Practice-Kit.zip)

## Ask three questions

Type each line separately. Press Enter after each one. The code block shows exactly what you type. The guest prints the answer underneath.

```sh
whoami
hostname
cat /etc/os-release
```

`whoami` names the account running the command, normally `learner`. `hostname` identifies the guest, normally `client` at the first console. `cat` displays the contents of a file. Find `ID` and `VERSION_ID` in `/etc/os-release`. They identify the distribution and release. Switch to the server and predict which of these three answers will change. Check your prediction, then return to the client.

## Install a machine yourself

The managed desktop route has already built the machines. To learn installation hands-on, use a separate empty training VM. Give it a new virtual disk, about 30 GiB, two virtual CPUs and about 4 GiB of memory. Attach the AlmaLinux DVD as installation media. Compare its SHA-256 digest with the published checksum for that exact image. Choose the VM's language, time zone and the new virtual disk by its capacity. Select automatic partitioning and a minimal or server environment. Create `learner` as an administrator. Complete installation, eject the installation media and boot the installed disk. Perform the same three checks. If the installer starts again, inspect the boot order and the attached media.

## Leave yourself a fresh start

**Stop lab** powers down the managed pair and keeps its disks. **Reset disks** discards the shared pair's practice changes. Save any notes you want to keep outside those disks first. On a manually built kit pair, use the reference to capture its ready baseline before using the kit's reset command. For a standalone VM, take a powered-off snapshot after testing your login.

**First handoff.** Write one line for the client and one for the server giving the host name, account and distribution. Explain which machine's files would change if you typed a command at the client prompt. If your evidence says Fedora, Windows or Debian instead of AlmaLinux, pause and identify which terminal you opened.

[AlmaLinux checksums and downloads](https://almalinux.org/get-almalinux/) · [RHEL 10 documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10)

lessons.title: Read a prompt and recover from a typing mistake
lessons.body:
In the desktop app, choose **Open practice terminal** alongside this reading, start the lab if needed, and log in at the client console.

A terminal carries keystrokes and output. A shell reads a line, splits it into words and starts a command. In a prompt such as `[learner@client ~]$`, learner is the account, client is the hostname, and the tilde stands for that user's home directory. The dollar sign is the prompt. Type the text that follows it in examples.

Start as your ordinary user. Type `pwd` and press Enter. It prints your working directory, often `/home/learner`. Type `ls -ld /etc`. The first word chooses the program. The option `-d` asks for the directory itself, and `-l` asks for its long listing. The last word is the object to inspect. Compare it with `ls /etc`, which lists the directory's children. You can read a system directory without having permission to change it.

## Learn to get unstuck
Type `printf '%s\n' 'night shift'`. The quotes group the two words into one argument. Use the Up arrow to recall that command and edit the text. Now type an opening single quote without a closing quote and press Enter. Bash gives a continuation prompt because the command is incomplete. Press Ctrl+C to cancel it. Run `sleep 30` and use Ctrl+C again to return to the prompt. For a long listing piped to `less`, press q to leave the pager.

**Read the evidence.** Run `ls /no-such-training-path` and then `echo $?`. A diagnostic names the missing path and the status is nonzero. Run `pwd` and immediately inspect the status again. Zero records success for that command. Each new command replaces the previous status.

**Try it independently.** Without retyping the successful listing, recall it and inspect /var. Show how you would tell the difference between a shell waiting for the rest of a quotation, a pager awaiting a key, and a command that has already failed and returned to the prompt.

lessons.title: Choose your workspace and identify both machines
lessons.body:
You are responsible for a small office's client and file server. Later a user will report a missing share, a failed login and a service that disappeared after reboot. A useful incident note starts with **where** you observed the failure and **as whom** you tested. Today you will make that baseline without changing either machine.

## Read each console
Open the shared practice terminal beside this lesson. In **Client console**, log in as `learner` using **Console login**. On a manual pair, use the account you created. Run these commands individually.

```console
> hostname
The name of the guest you opened.
> id
Your numeric user ID, primary group, and supplementary groups. Values vary.
> ip -brief address
One row per interface. The private client address is 192.168.77.20/24 in the supplied pair.
> cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
A UUID that changes after each boot.
```

Read `uid` as the numerical identity of your account and `groups` as the memberships held by this login. `ip -brief address` lists interfaces and addresses. Ignore `lo` for the private network comparison. The boot ID is a long identifier generated at each boot. A hostname can survive many reboots. A boot ID lets you prove that a service really worked after a restart.

Switch to **Server console** and gather the same four observations. In the supplied pair, the private server address is `192.168.77.10` and the private client address is `192.168.77.20`. Your own pair may use different addresses. Record actual values.

| Record | Client | Server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hostname and account | Fill from hostname and id | Fill from hostname and id |
| Private address and interface | Read the active interface | Read the active interface |
| Current boot | First eight characters of boot ID | First eight characters of boot ID |

## Work the course in three passes

On the first reading, predict one observable result and then run the worked example. Next, do the transfer ticket with its new filenames, accounts or values. Only then check the worked review or answer the quiz. Keep notes in your own notebook or outside the resettable guests. Use **Read your result and plan a targeted retake** after the final to choose the skill to repeat.

The shared workshop belongs to this course and learner. Navigate to another ordinary reading while it is open and run `pwd` or `hostname` again. A timed practical opens a different attempt. **Prepare machines** boots that attempt, and **Begin** starts its clock. Leaving a timed lesson keeps the deadline running. Stop idle pairs if your computer is short of memory. To repeat an assessment, use that practical's reset after saving any evidence you want.

**Independent handoff.** Give a partner two observations that would distinguish “wrong account,” “wrong guest,” and “right guest, different boot.” Show the command that produced each observation. A heading on the screen or a prompt by itself is weaker evidence than a command run inside the guest.

lessons.title: Predict what Bash will pass to a command
lessons.body:
You receive a request to print the names of every report in a directory. One report is called `night shift.txt`. A space is ordinary in a filename. At the prompt, an unquoted space separates arguments. An argument is one piece of information given to a command. Bash interprets the line before the program sees those arguments.

## Watch Bash do its work
On the client, as `learner`, make a fresh directory. `mktemp -d` creates one with a unique name, and `$(...)` substitutes its output. The assignment saves that name for this shell. Type one line at a time.

```console
> work=$(mktemp -d)

> cd "$work"

> touch 'night shift.txt' day.txt

> printf '<%s>\n' night shift.txt
<night>
<shift.txt>
> printf '<%s>\n' 'night shift.txt'
<night shift.txt>
> printf '<%s>\n' *.txt
<day.txt>
<night shift.txt>
```

The first print produces two lines. The second prints one. In the third, Bash expands the wildcard into two filenames before starting `printf`. Each matches one argument, including the name with a space. Try quoting `'*.txt'` and explain why the star itself reaches the program. `touch` created two empty files, so counting their bytes would tell you nothing about how many names matched.

Set `ticket='night shift.txt'`. Compare `printf '<%s>\n' "$ticket"` with `printf '<%s>\n' '$ticket'`. Double quotes allow variable expansion and keep its result together. Single quotes preserve the characters you typed. Type `type cd` and `type -a ls`. Bash handles some commands itself and finds other programs using the directories in `PATH`. When a command fails, first check the spelling with `type` and its inputs with `printf`.

## Take the next ticket
Create a third file named `night cover.txt`. List just the two night filenames, one per line, then print the same wildcard literally. Arrange both results before reading on.

**Check your work.** An unquoted `night*.txt` expands to two names. Quoting that pattern produces one line containing a star. Your original directory should still contain three files. Return to your home directory with `cd`. The variable disappears when you log out, while the files remain until the temporary directory is cleaned.

lessons.title: Find the right manual when you forget an option
lessons.body:
A colleague asks you how to show the permissions of a directory itself. You remember `ls`, but a normal listing shows its children. An administrator needs a way to recover forgotten syntax inside the guest. Documentation is part of your working environment.

## Look up an answer, then test it
On the client, run `ls --help | less`. The pipe feeds the help text into a pager. Type `/directory` and press Enter to search, use `n` to find the next occurrence, and press `q` to return to the shell. Now run `man ls` and find the long option `--directory`. Compare these observations.

```sh
ls /etc | head -n 3
ls -ld /etc
man -w ls
rpm -qd coreutils | head
```

The second listing describes one directory. Its initial `d` tells you the file type. `man -w` reports where the manual comes from. `rpm -qd` lists documentation shipped by that RPM. A minimal installation may split manuals into separate packages. Use `command --help` and `ls /usr/share/doc` when a page is absent. For Bash builtins, try `help cd` inside Bash. For a GNU program with a full manual, run `info coreutils`, follow a menu entry with Enter and leave with `q` when Info and its manuals are installed.

Manual section numbers distinguish different things with the same name. Compare `man 1 passwd` and `man 5 passwd`. One describes the password-changing program. The other describes a file format. Read the heading and the synopsis before accepting an example.

## Find an unfamiliar option
Use local documentation to work out how `sort` compares numbers. Feed it the lines 12, 3 and 21. Capture the original order, the default sort and the numeric sort. Explain the difference to someone who thinks 12 is smaller than 3.

**Check your work.** `printf '%s\n' 12 3 21 | sort -n` prints 3, 12, 21. Plain `sort` compares text according to the locale. Record the documentation heading and the flag that settled the question. This is the lookup routine to use in the later independent practical.

lessons.title: Find your way through a Linux filesystem
lessons.body:
A pathname describes a walk through directories. An absolute path starts at the root directory, written /. A relative path starts at the process's current directory. Each shell has its own working directory. A colleague's instruction to “edit reports/today” is ambiguous until you know where they started.

## Make a work area
Open a regular-user terminal. Work in a fresh directory. Use `mkdir -p ~/shift-practice/inbox ~/shift-practice/archive` and `cd ~/shift-practice`. The shell expands ~ to your home directory. Run `pwd` and `ls -a`. A single dot refers to this directory and two dots to its parent. Create an empty file with `touch 'inbox/shift notes'`, then try `ls -l 'inbox/shift notes'`. Move into inbox and ask Bash for the same path again. From here that relative path asks for an inbox *inside* inbox. Use `ls -l 'shift notes'` to identify the same file.

## Give the next shift a copy
From inbox run `cp 'shift notes' ../archive/day-one`. Rename the original with `mv 'shift notes' 'shift report'`. List both directories. A copy has its own content and name. Renaming the source leaves the copy's name alone. Use `ls -ld /etc /var /home /run`. Configuration commonly lives in /etc, changing service data in /var, personal work in /home and runtime state in /run. Remember where to look when a setting disappears on restart.

**Independent ticket.** Starting in your home directory, put a second copy of day-one in inbox under the name day-two. Remove only day-two with `rm -i` and confirm what still exists with `find ~/shift-practice -type f`. Your two original files should remain. If a pathname contains spaces, quote the whole pathname or use Tab completion. A missing-file error gives you a pathname to check before changing privileges.

lessons.title: Recover from a renamed file using links and inodes
lessons.body:
An application opens a file called `current`. An operator renames an old report, and suddenly one shortcut breaks while another still works. To predict which one, separate a directory entry (a name) from the filesystem record that holds the file's metadata and refers to its data. That record has an inode number within its filesystem.

## Change the name; observe the object
Run this in a new client practice directory. Read each listing before running the next line.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$work"
printf 'shift 1\n' > original
ln original second-name
ln -s original current
ls -li
mv original archived
ls -li
cat second-name
readlink current
cat current
```

The first two ordinary names had the same inode number and a link count of two. A hard link is another name for the same object. The symbolic link has its own inode and contains the path `original`. Renaming the target leaves that text untouched. `readlink current` can therefore succeed while `cat current` reports a missing target. A relative target is resolved from the directory containing the symbolic link.

Write `printf 'shift 2\n' >> archived` and read `second-name`. Both names expose the new line. Make a plain copy using `cp archived frozen`. Append another line through `second-name`. Compare `wc -l archived second-name frozen`. The copy stops following changes once it is made.

## Repair the handoff
Make `current` resolve to `archived` while preserving both ordinary names and the independent copy. Test the contents through each of the four names. Predict what will happen if the original directory is copied to another filesystem.

**Check your work.** Remove only your dangling symlink with `unlink current` and recreate it using `ln -s archived current`. Run `ls -li` and `cmp archived current`. Compare inode numbers only within the same filesystem. A hard link cannot span filesystems. A symlink can span them if its target path still resolves.

lessons.title: Edit a configuration and find help offline
lessons.body:
Many system settings are text files. An editor changes the file on disk. A service may keep using its previously loaded settings until you reload it. First practice where a typo affects only your home directory.

Run `mkdir -p ~/editor-practice` and `cd ~/editor-practice`. Create a known starting point with `printf 'owner=morning\nqueue=1\n' > shift.conf`. Make a backup with `cp -p shift.conf shift.conf.before`. Open `vi shift.conf`. In normal mode type `/morning` and press Enter to find the word. Press `cw`, type `evening`, press Esc and type `:wq` followed by Enter. If you get lost before saving, Esc then `:q!` discards that edit. Compare files with `diff -u shift.conf.before shift.conf`. Lines with minus and plus show the old and new values. An exit status of one from diff means the files differ.

For a command whose options you have forgotten, ask the installed manual. Open `man cp`, search for `/preserve`, use n for the next match and q to quit. Compare `man 1 passwd` (the program) with `man 5 passwd` (the account record format). Use `info coreutils` where installed. Locate package documents with `rpm -qd coreutils` and inspect `/usr/share/doc`. A minimal image may need man-db, man-pages, info or package documentation installed from its configured source.

**Independent ticket.** Add a third line, `region=west`, without changing the first two. Show the exact change in a diff, then restore the original from your backup. Run `cmp shift.conf.before shift.conf` and inspect its status. A silent successful comparison is a useful receipt.

lessons.title: Follow data through a pipeline
lessons.body:
A program can read standard input and write to two places: its ordinary output and its diagnostic output. A pipe carries the first program's standard output into the next program's standard input. This lets one person write a filter and another decide where its results should go.

In a fresh directory under your home, create a small shift log.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '08:00 OK bay-1' '08:10 ERROR bay-2' '08:20 OK bay-2' '08:30 ERROR bay-3' > shift.log
grep ' ERROR ' shift.log
grep ' ERROR ' shift.log | wc -l
```

The first pipeline stage selects whole lines. The second counts newline characters, so expect two. Try `grep '^08:10' shift.log`. The caret anchors the match at the beginning. Compare `grep -E 'bay-[23]$' shift.log` with `grep -F 'bay-[23]$' shift.log`. The first interprets the character class and end anchor. The second looks for those literal characters. Keep shell quotes around a pattern so the shell passes it to grep unchanged.

## Decide what to keep
Run `grep ' ERROR ' shift.log > alerts` twice. The second run replaces the old output. Add one line using `printf '%s\n' 'manually reviewed' >> alerts`; the double angle brackets append. Now run `cat shift.log missing-file > collected 2> diagnostics`. Read both new files. The valid lines survived even though one input failed. A nonempty output file by itself cannot certify a successful run.

**Independent ticket.** Produce a file containing just the bay-2 events, in time order, and a separate count. Predict both lines before checking. Search for a bay you know is absent and immediately inspect grep's exit status. Status 1 means no match; a missing input file typically gives status 2. Decide whether each deserves the same alert.

lessons.title: Read a log without counting the wrong records
lessons.body:
An overnight report needs the disk incidents from node 2. An operator searched for `disk` and counted every mention, including a recovery message. A useful search describes the exact records of interest. `grep` selects complete input lines. An extended regular expression describes their structure. A shell wildcard selects pathnames before the command runs.

## Build evidence small enough to inspect
Make a disposable directory on the client. The here-document sends the lines between two `EVENTS` markers to `cat`. Quote the first marker so the shell preserves its contents.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$work"
cat > events <<'EVENTS'
node2 WARN disk busy
node2 INFO disk recovered
node20 WARN disk busy
node2 WARN link down
node2 ERROR disk offline
EVENTS
grep disk events
grep -En '^node2 (WARN|ERROR) disk ' events
```

You should see lines 1 and 5 in the second result. The caret anchors the start. The space after `node2` prevents `node20` from matching. Parentheses group alternatives in extended mode. The final space separates the word `disk` from its message. The `-n` flag shows original line numbers, which lets a colleague reproduce your finding. Quotes make the expression one shell argument.

Use `grep -Ec '^node2 (WARN|ERROR) disk ' events` to count selected lines. Then try an expression that finds nothing and immediately issue `echo $?`. A status of 1 means no selected lines. Try reading a missing filename and inspect its status and error message. An unreadable input and a quiet system are different conclusions. An empty output file alone cannot tell you which happened.

## Investigate another incident
Add a disk warning for node20 and an informational message for node2. Produce a report containing only node20 disk warnings and a separate file for diagnostics. Confirm the number of records and explain why an unanchored search would be risky if names/prefixes overlap.

**Check your work.** A pattern beginning `^node20 WARN disk ` matches exactly two records after your addition. Redirect selected lines with `> report` and diagnostics with `2> errors`. A successful run leaves the latter empty. Check the return status before running a different command.

lessons.title: Deliver a backup another operator can really restore
lessons.body:
A compressed file sitting on a disk is a promise. Test that promise by restoring the files to an empty directory and comparing their contents. An archive holds names, directory structure and metadata. Compression reduces the bytes used to store the archive. This distinction matters when deciding how to unpack a handoff.

## Build and restore a shift packet
Use the client as `learner`. `-C` gives tar a directory to work from, so the archive stores relative names that another account can restore elsewhere.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$work"
mkdir -p packet/logs restore-gz restore-bz
printf 'bay 4\n' > packet/logs/evening
printf 'ready\n' > packet/status
tar -czf shift.tar.gz -C packet .
tar -tjf shift.tar.gz
```

That last command deliberately selects the bzip2 decoder for a gzip file. Read the error. The source packet still exists. Use `file shift.tar.gz` if available to identify its format. In `-czf`, `c` creates an archive, `z` selects gzip and `f` takes the filename. Replace `c` with `t` to list it or `x` to extract it.

```sh
tar -tzf shift.tar.gz
tar -xzf shift.tar.gz -C restore-gz
diff -r packet restore-gz
tar -cjf shift.tar.bz2 -C packet .
tar -xjf shift.tar.bz2 -C restore-bz
diff -r packet restore-bz
```

Both comparisons should be silent and return zero. `tar -t` verifies readable member names. `diff -r` also checks whether the restored content matches. Perform a restore into an empty destination so existing files cannot mask missing members. Inspect an archive's member list before extracting it.

## Hand off an independent restore
Add a file whose name includes a space to the source. Create a fresh archive in either format, then restore it into a third empty directory without modifying the source. Give the next operator the format, the relative member name and an observation establishing an exact restore.

**Check your work.** The member list contains the new name once. `diff -r` reports no difference, and `sha256sum` on the new source and restored file prints identical digests. Leave the two older archives intact and explain why neither contains this later file.

lessons.title: Predict who can read, change or enter a path
lessons.body:
Linux checks the caller's identity against the file's owner, group and other permission classes. Read the first character of `ls -l` for the file type, then the three permission triplets. For a regular file, r reads data, w changes data and x permits execution. For a directory, r lists names, x traverses to a known entry, and w with x allows changes to directory entries. Deleting a file is a change to its parent directory.

Run the following as your ordinary user in an empty directory you own. The parentheses start a subshell so the changed umask lasts only for this exercise.

```sh
(umask 027; mkdir crew; touch crew/notes; stat -c '%a %n' crew crew/notes)
chmod u=rw,g=r,o= crew/notes
ls -ld crew crew/notes
```

A new ordinary file commonly starts from requested mode 666, a directory from 777. A mask of 027 removes group write and all permissions for others. Expect 640 for notes and 750 for crew. A mask removes bits from what was requested, so it cannot grant execute permission to a new ordinary file. Existing objects keep their earlier mode.

**Diagnose one failure.** Temporarily remove your own search permission with `chmod u-x crew`. Predict whether `cat crew/notes` works. Run it, then `namei -l "$PWD/crew/notes"` to inspect every path component. Restore traversal with `chmod u+x crew`. Confirm the file is still 640. An administrator testing as root can miss this denial.

**Independent ticket.** Give the owner read/write, group read, and others no access on a second file using numeric mode. Set the parent directory so its group can enter and list it. Explain why group members who can list the filename might still fail to open the file.

lessons.title: Independent shift: restore an operator's handoff
lessons.body:
Your first independent assignment combines the shell, a text editor, filters, permissions and archives. Work as `learner` on the untimed client. Use local manuals freely. Read the work order before looking at the review below. The goal is to leave another operator a verifiable result. Every run starts with a new folder.

## The intake
Create an empty working directory with `mktemp -d` and save its path. In it, create a file `arrivals` containing these four lines in this order:

```text
east OPEN drive
west CLOSED tray
east OPEN cable
east CLOSED drive
```

The receiving operator wants a directory called `handoff`. Inside it put a file `east-open` containing only open east tickets in their original order. Give the file owner read/write, group read, and others no access. Include a relative symbolic link `today` pointing to that file. Create a gzip-compressed tar archive containing the contents of `handoff`. Deliver it by restoring into a separate empty directory. Keep your original input.

## Evidence to hand back
Award yourself one check for each observable outcome: the two correct records in order, the requested file mode, a relative link that works in the restored directory, and a restore whose contents match the original. If a check fails, note the symptom and repair that part before starting over. Repeat once on fresh inputs by substituting west and CLOSED for east and OPEN. The second run is the transfer test.

## Worked review
One solution is `grep '^east OPEN ' arrivals > handoff/east-open` after creating `handoff`. Inspect the file before setting mode 640. Run `ln -s east-open handoff/today`; constructing that target relative to the link makes the restored copy portable. Use `tar -czf shift.tar.gz -C handoff .`, list its members, then extract with `tar -xzf shift.tar.gz -C restored` after creating `restored`. Compare `readlink restored/today`, `stat -c '%a' restored/east-open`, `cat restored/today` and `diff -r handoff restored`. A listing alone cannot establish that the restored symlink resolves to the right data.

lessons.title: Understand a login, a group and a privileged command
lessons.body:
A login name is the human label for a numeric user ID. Permissions use the numeric identity. A process also carries a primary group and may carry extra groups. Two machines may have the same login name and different users behind it. Start on the client and run `whoami`, `id` and `getent passwd "$(id -un)"`. Read the account name, numeric IDs, home directory and login shell from the colon-separated account record. The x in the password field tells you that password verification data is stored separately.

Run `sudo -l` and read which commands your account may request. Use `sudo id -u` if allowed. It prints 0 when that single command runs as root. Follow it with `id -u` to see your original shell identity. To test another account's view on your own VM, start a new login shell with `sudo -iu learner` from an authorized administrator account. Compare `pwd`, `id` and `printf '%s\n' "$HOME"`, then `exit` to return. A new shell is a separate process and inherits a set of credentials at startup.

**Worked diagnosis.** You add a person to an existing group. The account database immediately lists both groups when you run `id USERNAME`. In their open terminal, plain `id` still shows the earlier list. Ask them to start a fresh login and repeat both checks. Changing ownership on every team file would address a different problem.

**Independent ticket.** On the client, find learner's login shell and primary group. In a fresh learner session, identify the effective user for a privileged read-only command. Record which machine answered. Explain why that result tells you nothing about who may run the same command on the server.

lessons.title: See what changes when you become another user
lessons.body:
The same terminal can run programs with different permissions. A login session has a user ID, group IDs, a home directory and an environment. The kernel uses numeric identities to decide which operations the process may perform. A friendly name is a lookup for a number. Being allowed to use `sudo` gives you a way to request a particular privileged action.

## Observe three contexts
Use the ordinary learner account on the practice client. Start in its home directory. In the first command below, `-u` selects the effective user ID and `-n` asks for its name. Write down each answer before moving on.

```sh
whoami
id
printf '%s\n' "$HOME"
pwd
sudo id
whoami
```

`sudo id` reports the identity of the child process as root when the policy allows it. The second `whoami` still prints learner. If a password is requested, type the learner password at the console prompt. On these training guests some commands may be authorized without a password. Inspect `sudo -l` to learn which policy applies to this account.

Now run `sudo -iu root` inside the disposable guest. Run the same identity, home and working-directory checks. A login shell normally starts in the target account's home with that account's environment. Use `exit` exactly once, then check `whoami` again. Keep the narrowest privilege you need for the following exercises. For example, a regular user can inspect `ls -ld /etc` without privilege.

## Explain a failed write
From learner's shell, try creating a unique practice file under your own home and listing it with `ls -ln`. Translate the numeric owner using `id -u`. Then inspect the ownership and permissions of `/etc` without changing anything there. Explain why those two directories permit different actions. If `sudo echo text > file` fails for a privileged destination, which program tried to open the destination?

**Check your reasoning.** Bash arranges redirections before it starts `sudo`. A privileged writer such as `sudo tee` can open an approved destination itself. Save edits to real system configuration for the later lessons, where you will test the resulting settings and restore them.

lessons.title: Onboard an operator without losing existing access
lessons.body:
An operator should join a second team without losing an earlier assignment. On the untimed client, use spare names for this exercise. Check `getent passwd fieldops`, `getent group dispatch`, `getent group editors-local` and `getent group editors-night` first. On a fresh guest the names should be unused.

```sh
sudo groupadd dispatch
sudo groupadd editors-local
sudo useradd -m -G dispatch fieldops
sudo usermod -aG editors-local fieldops
id fieldops
sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 fieldops
sudo chage -l fieldops
sudo -iu fieldops id
```

Expect both supplementary groups and a 90-day maximum age. `usermod -G` replaces the supplementary list unless you append. Existing shells keep their group credentials until a new login. Set a password interactively with `sudo passwd fieldops` and verify the aging policy again. Avoid putting passwords in shell history. Rename a group with `groupmod -n NEW OLD`, lock an account with `usermod -L` and unlock it with `usermod -U`. Change a primary group with `usermod -g`; that does not touch supplementary groups.

## Rename a group and verify its identity

Record the numeric GID from `getent group editors-local`. Run `sudo groupmod -n editors-night editors-local` and compare `getent group editors-night`, `getent group editors-local` and `id fieldops`. Expect the same GID and the same membership under the new name. The old name should no longer resolve. What happens to a file owned by this GID?

## Delegate one administrative action
Locate `systemctl` with `command -v systemctl`. Use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status` to grant the exact command (adjust its path if necessary).

```text
fieldops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl is-active chronyd.service
```

Run `sudo visudo -c` and `sudo -l -U fieldops`. Compare the granted command and arguments to the request. To retire only this practice identity, remove the new sudoers entry, run `sudo userdel -r fieldops`, then check that the practice groups are empty and run `sudo groupdel editors-night` and `sudo groupdel dispatch`. Verify the lookups now return no record. A local account or group on the client has a separate database from one with the same name on the server.

lessons.title: Predict who can create, read or remove a file
lessons.body:
A team member can read an existing report but cannot save a replacement. Many programs save by creating a new file and renaming it. Reading the old file and changing its parent directory require different permissions. On a directory, read lists names, execute searches through known names and write changes directory entries when traversal is allowed.

## Separate a file from its parent
Run the following as the ordinary learner on the client. `mktemp` gives this run a new disposable location.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir "$work/inbox"
printf 'ready\n' > "$work/inbox/report"
chmod 400 "$work/inbox/report"
chmod 500 "$work/inbox"
cat "$work/inbox/report"
touch "$work/inbox/new"
```

The read succeeds. The new file fails because the directory owner has read and execute but lacks write. Change the directory to mode 700. Try `mv "$work/inbox/report" "$work/inbox/closed"`. Renaming should now succeed, even though the file itself is read-only. Check `ls -ld` on the directory and `ls -l` on the file before explaining the result. Do these tests without `sudo` so the result reflects the learner's access.

A creation mask removes bits from the mode a program requests when creating an object. Observe it in a subshell so you can try different defaults without changing your login setup.

```sh
(umask 027; touch "$work/ordinary"; mkdir "$work/folder")
stat -c '%a %n' "$work/ordinary" "$work/folder"
```

On this fresh directory without a default ACL, expect 640 for the file and 750 for the directory. Programs normally request 666 for ordinary files and 777 for directories. A mask of 027 clears group write and all permissions for others. Existing files keep their old modes.

## Take the access ticket
Create a second directory whose new files are readable and writable only by the owner. Have the same account create a file inside and show its numeric mode. Make the parent temporarily inaccessible for traversal, predict `cat` on the known file, then restore owner traversal and compare.

**Check your work.** `(umask 077; touch ... )` in the fresh directory produces mode 600 for an ordinary file. `namei -l` on the file path displays each directory along the way. Record the first component that stopped traversal and the single change that restored access.

lessons.title: Find evidence and build a shared directory
lessons.body:
A colleague reports that overnight copies failed. Work as learner on the untimed client. Choose an unused directory name for this run. Make a private practice directory and turn a noisy log into an archive someone else can inspect.

```sh
install -d -m 700 ~/rhcsa-tools && cd ~/rhcsa-tools
printf '%s\n' 'OK copied' 'ERR read' 'OK copied' 'ERR write' > run.log
grep '^ERR ' run.log | sort > errors.txt
wc -l < errors.txt
ln run.log run.hard
ln -s run.log run.link
ls -li run*
tar -czf evidence.tar.gz run.log errors.txt
tar -tzf evidence.tar.gz
```

Expect two errors, the same inode for the two hard-linked names, and a symbolic link containing a pathname. Rename `run.log` to `night.log`. Predict which link still reads the log, then test each. Capture the failed read with `cat run.link 2>link-error.txt`. Restore the name and verify the symbolic link works again. Create a bzip2 version with `tar -cjf evidence.tar.bz2 run.log` after restoring the name. Run `mkdir from-gzip from-bzip2`. Extract the archives with `tar -xzf evidence.tar.gz -C from-gzip` and `tar -xjf evidence.tar.bz2 -C from-bzip2`. Check both restored copies with `cmp run.log from-gzip/run.log` and `cmp run.log from-bzip2/run.log`. Both should exit zero. Look up flags using `man tar`, `info coreutils` or `/usr/share/doc`.

## A directory shared by a team
On the server, create a practice group with `sudo groupadd editors` if absent. Run `sudo install -d -g editors -m 2770 /srv/editorial`. With `stat -c '%A %a %G' /srv/editorial` expect `drwxrws--- 2770 editors`. Directory execute permission allows traversal. Setgid makes newly created children inherit the directory's group. It does not grant write permission by itself.

Try it with `sudo touch /srv/editorial/draft` and inspect the group on the child. If a user cannot enter a path despite suitable final permissions, inspect every ancestor with `namei -l /srv/editorial/draft`. In a clean practice directory, try `cp`, `mv`, a text editor, and `rm -i` on your own disposable file to practice the file lifecycle.

## Search text and redirect streams
Regular expressions select lines by pattern. `grep -E '^(ERR|WARN) ' run.log` matches lines that start with either word. In basic syntax without `-E`, `|` and parentheses are literal characters unless escaped. Add `-v` to invert the match, `-c` to count matching lines, `-i` to ignore case and `-n` to show line numbers. Anchors `^` and `$` mark the start and end of a line.

`>` replaces a file and `>>` appends. `2>` sends standard error elsewhere. Redirections apply left to right, so `command >> all.log 2>&1` appends both streams, while `command 2>&1 >> all.log` still sends errors to the terminal. A pipe `|` connects standard output only.

To act as another user in a full login environment run `su - USER`, or `sudo -i -u USER` where sudo policy allows it. `su` without `-` keeps much of your current environment, including the working directory. Leave the other user's shell with `exit`.

lessons.title: Lab • Hand off a team workspace
lessons.body:
On the **server**, prepare `/srv/team` for `labops`. This group is local to the server. Create it here if needed. Team members need full directory access, others need none, and new entries should inherit the team group. The requested final mode is `2770`.

Before submission, inspect the directory itself, create a disposable child inside it, and check the child's group. Remove your test child. If the mode reads `0770`, identify which special bit is missing. If the group is wrong only on a child created earlier, repeat with a new file. Submit when the directory is correct and review the post-reboot result.

## Reason through a reported result
A teammate can enter /srv/team, but a newly created note belongs to the writer’s primary group. The directory listing reads drwxrwx---. Which observation explains this?

**Check your reasoning.** Group write and search work, but the directory lacks the setgid bit. Inspect the directory itself, then create a new child after repair. Existing files keep their previous group.

lessons.title: Lab • Add a client operator
lessons.body:
On the **client**, create the local account `labtech` and give it membership in `labops`. Preserve any other membership the account has. The group on the server belongs to the other guest and cannot grant access here. Create a local `labops` group on the client if `getent group labops` finds none.

Check `getent passwd labtech`, `getent group labops` and `id labtech`. A blank member list in a group record can still be consistent with a primary group, so judge effective membership with `id`. Switch to a fresh login context to see the groups a new process would receive. Submit and compare the membership checks across the reboot.

## Reason through a reported result
A fresh client login lists labops, while an older labtech shell still lists its previous groups. Which result should you trust for the next login?

**Check your reasoning.** The fresh login has the new process credentials. Check the account database as well. Existing shells keep their previous supplementary groups.

lessons.title: Follow one connection from client to service
lessons.body:
Imagine that a browser on the client asks the server for a report. It needs an address for the server, a route to that address, a listening service at a port, and permission for the traffic to reach it. Each question has a different observer. Start at the client for name and route. Inspect the server for a listener and its firewall.

An IPv4 address such as 192.168.77.20 identifies an interface on this network. The /24 prefix describes its network portion. The client can ordinarily reach 192.168.77.10 directly on the same private network. To reach a different network, it usually sends to a gateway. An IPv6 example, 2001:db8:42::20/64, uses the same address-and-prefix idea with more bits. A port identifies an application endpoint on an address. Resolving a name proves only that an address was returned.

## Draw your two machines
On each guest run `hostname` and `ip -br address`. Label the interfaces, addresses and prefixes in a two-row table. The lo interface and 127.0.0.1 or ::1 point back to the current guest. Ask the client which path it would use with `ip route get 192.168.77.10`. Read the device and source address. An answer to this command is the kernel's route choice; it does not send a request to the server.

On the server run `ss -lnt`. If SSH is running, look for TCP port 22 and read the address to its left. A service bound only to 127.0.0.1 accepts local connections. A listener bound to 0.0.0.0 accepts connections addressed to any local IPv4 interface, subject to firewall and service policy.

**Independent ticket.** The file server resolves to 127.0.0.1 on the client. The server shows a healthy listener. Explain which machine the client actually contacted. Use `getent hosts` with the reported name, compare both address inventories, and describe the smallest correction. In the next lesson you will persist a hostname mapping and a separate dual-stack interface profile.

lessons.title: Read an address, a route and a connection profile
lessons.body:
Your client and server live on one virtual Ethernet link. An interface is the guest's endpoint on that link. An IP address identifies a destination at the network layer. A prefix marks the shared network portion of an address. On the lab's IPv4 `/24`, the first 24 bits (the first three octets) identify the network. The client at `192.168.77.20` and the server at `192.168.77.10` therefore share a subnet. A default gateway matters when no more specific route matches.

## Predict the path before sending a packet
Use the client console. A loopback address, such as `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, sends traffic back to this guest. Find the other interface carrying the client lab address.

```sh
ip -brief link
ip -brief address
ip route show
ip route get 192.168.77.10
nmcli device status
nmcli connection show --active
```

Read the `dev` and `src` fields from the route lookup. They identify the outgoing interface and chosen source. A peer on the directly attached prefix generally needs no router. Compare the interface name with the active NetworkManager profile on that device. A device can be called `enp1s0` while its saved profile has a descriptive name. Record the actual values from your guest. A lab without an external default route can still reach its private peer.

IPv6 also uses prefixes. A `/64` leaves 64 bits for the interface identifier. A short address containing `::` omits a run of zero groups. Link-local addresses beginning with `fe80:` apply to one link, so an interface matters when choosing their scope. Use `ip -6 address show` and `ip -6 route show` to inspect the available IPv6 information. The following lesson creates a dummy interface so you can configure IPv4 and IPv6 without changing the connection to the lab server.

## Trace a report from the right guest
Without changing either machine, find the route back to the client from the server. Then compare `getent hosts localhost` on the two guests and explain why the results alone cannot identify the other machine. Use `ping -c 2 192.168.77.10` on the client if the network permits ICMP. A failed ping alone does not establish that an application port is closed.

**Check your work.** The peer-facing source on the server is .10 and on the client is .20. A correct handoff names the source, destination and interface for each direction and distinguishes a live route from a saved connection profile.

lessons.title: Trace a request from name to interface to listener
lessons.body:
A user can reach a file server by address but cannot reach it by name. Test the same name lookup the application uses before changing routes. On the client compare `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test`, `ip route get 192.168.77.10` and `ip -brief address`. On the server inspect listening TCP sockets with `ss -lnt`. A resolver failure, missing route and closed listener have different remedies.

Add `192.168.77.10 server.workshop.test` once to the client's `/etc/hosts`, then run `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u`. Expect one unique address. Multiple rows for stream and datagram socket types are normal. Check `grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf` to see where applications look up hosts. `dig` queries DNS directly and may miss a valid local hosts entry.

## Configure a practice interface without changing the lab link
In the untimed client with NetworkManager available, create a dummy profile. Check that `workshop-dummy` and `dummy42` are unused first.

```sh
sudo nmcli connection add type dummy ifname dummy42 con-name workshop-dummy ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.44/24 ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:42::44/64
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy connection.autoconnect yes
sudo nmcli connection up workshop-dummy
ip -brief address show dummy42
nmcli -f connection.autoconnect,ipv4.addresses,ipv6.addresses connection show workshop-dummy
```

Verify both addresses and the autoconnect setting. Reboot the workshop guest and verify again. Keep the profile for the next exercise. Keep the engine-provided interface unchanged. A connection profile persists configuration; commands such as `ip addr add` change runtime state.

## Change an existing profile and the hostname
Tasks usually modify the profile that already exists for an interface. Find it with `nmcli connection show` and `nmcli device status`. Practice on the dummy profile before you remove it:

```sh
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy ipv4.never-default yes ipv6.never-default yes
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy +ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.45/24
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy +ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:42::45/64
sudo nmcli connection up workshop-dummy
nmcli -f ipv4,ipv6 connection show workshop-dummy | grep -E 'addresses|never-default'
```

`+` adds to a list property instead of replacing it. A change to a profile takes effect when the connection is activated again. Profiles are stored as keyfiles under `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections`; `nmtui` edits the same profiles interactively. NetworkManager writes `/etc/resolv.conf` from active profiles, so DNS servers belong in the profile rather than a hand edit of that file.

Set a persistent static hostname with `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname NAME` and check it with `hostnamectl` and a new login. The `hostname` command alone changes only the running system. Restore the guest's original hostname when you finish, because the course uses it to tell the guests apart.

When both addresses have been verified, remove only the dummy profile using `sudo nmcli connection delete workshop-dummy`. Verify the private lab route with `ip route get 192.168.77.10`.

lessons.title: Lab • Make the file server discoverable
lessons.body:
On the **client**, make `files.lab.test` consistently resolve to the server at `192.168.77.10` for IPv4 applications, including after startup. Preserve the existing localhost and guest mappings.

Look up the exact name with `getent ahostsv4` and list its distinct addresses. A ping to the numeric IP only tests a different part of the path. If two different addresses appear, inspect the matching hosts entries and the resolver order. Recheck with a fresh command before submitting.

## Reason through a reported result
A direct-address SSH connection works, but getent ahostsv4 files.lab.test returns nothing. Which layer will you change?

**Check your reasoning.** IP connectivity is already demonstrated. Check the client’s name-service order and its persistent mapping for the exact hostname, then repeat the application lookup.

lessons.title: Lab • Configure a second interface and the hostname
lessons.body:
The client has a second network interface with MAC address `52:54:00:aa:01:20`. It has no peer, so nothing answers on it; the grader checks configuration, not reachability. Leave the `192.168.77.20` lab link unchanged, or you will lose the server.

On the **client**:

1. Configure the second interface persistently with IPv4 address `10.88.10.20/24`, gateway `10.88.10.1` and DNS server `10.88.10.53`.
2. Set the hostname to `client01.lab.test`.

Match the MAC to an interface name with `ip -brief link`. `nmcli connection show` lists the profile cloud-init created for it; modify that profile, or create one bound to the interface, with `ipv4.method manual`. Bring it up and check `ip -brief address`, `nmcli -g IP4.GATEWAY,IP4.DNS device show IFACE` and `hostnamectl`. The new DNS server cannot answer, so `/etc/hosts` entries keep the lab names working.

The grader checks the address and prefix on that interface, the gateway and DNS NetworkManager applied, and the static hostname, then repeats after a reboot. Restore the original hostname afterward if you reuse this pair for other lessons.

lessons.title: Follow software from a trusted source to an installed file
lessons.body:
A user asks for the program that inspects a directory tree. Your system can answer three different questions. The shell can locate an executable on its search path. The RPM database can tell you which installed package owns a file. DNF can query available repositories to find software even before installation. A successful repository listing alone installs nothing.

Run `command -v bash`, `rpm -q bash` and `rpm -ql bash | head`. Write one sentence for each result. Compare `rpm -q tree` with `dnf info tree` on an AlmaLinux guest with BaseOS and AppStream enabled. DNF might show a candidate version while RPM reports no installed package. If DNF cannot find metadata, inspect `dnf repolist --enabled`, the source URL and whether that AlmaLinux guest can reach its mirror or has matching installation media attached.

## Observe a transaction
On your disposable guest with a working source, select a small optional package that is not already installed, such as tree. Run `sudo dnf install tree`. Read the transaction summary before accepting. Check `rpm -q tree`, run `tree --version`, and ask `rpm -qf "$(command -v tree)"` which package supplied it. Try `dnf check-update tree`; status 100 means updates are available. When a newer build exists, apply `sudo dnf upgrade tree` and compare versions. Use `sudo dnf remove tree` to retire your practice installation and inspect the removal summary before confirming. Restore the previous state if you started with a different package.

AlmaLinux uses distribution mirrors. Red Hat’s CDN serves signed RHEL packages to a registered, entitled RHEL machine. Practice the RHEL-specific registration steps in the manual-pair reference if you have access to RHEL. An internal RPM repository can use an approved HTTPS URL. The repository root must contain its repodata directory. A local RPM file also needs trusted signing keys and available dependencies. A Flatpak remote distributes applications and runtimes separately from the host RPM database. User-scope commands act for the account that runs them.

**Independent ticket.** One learner can launch a Flatpak application and a second account cannot find it. Predict what `flatpak list --user --app` in each login and `flatpak list --system --app` will show. Explain how you would select the intended scope before installing a second copy. Use the next workshop to add the remote and prove installation and removal.

lessons.title: Install and remove a signed package from the lab DVD
lessons.body:
A ticket asks you to make the `tree` directory viewer available on a disconnected client. The RPM file contains the payload and metadata. An RPM repository also provides a searchable index. DNF resolves dependencies and proposes a transaction. An empty repository with valid metadata can refresh successfully while offering no packages to install.

## Identify the available software
Use the untimed client. The AlmaLinux DVD provides BaseOS and AppStream packages on the prepared pair. Inspect `findmnt -t iso9660` and `dnf repolist --all`. If working on a manual VM, attach its verified AlmaLinux 10 DVD and mount it read-only before continuing. Use `lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS` to find the DVD containing BaseOS and AppStream. The small practice-kit disc is a separate device. Substitute the actual DVD mountpoint below.

```sh
dvd=/mnt/erudior-dvd
find "$dvd" -type f -name 'tree-[0-9]*.rpm'
rpm -q tree
```

Set `pkg` to the full pathname printed for the RPM matching the guest's architecture. If the search is empty, correct the mountpoint. Read `rpm -qp --qf '%{NAME} %{VERSION} %{ARCH}\n' "$pkg"` to inspect that file without installing it. Run `rpmkeys --checksig --verbose "$pkg"`. Compare the signing identity with the trusted AlmaLinux media/key on this guest. A missing trusted key or failed signature is a reason to check the source before proceeding.

## Carry out the request
Use a fresh practice client where `rpm -q tree` says tree is absent. Record that baseline. Run `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --setopt=localpkg_gpgcheck=1 install "$pkg"` and read the proposed changes. With dependencies already present, the verified local file is sufficient. If DNF reports a missing dependency, use the trusted DVD repositories or install the matching signed dependency from the same media. Review the transaction before confirming. Test the actual tool with `tree -L 1 /etc | head` and query `rpm -qf "$(command -v tree)"`. Finish by reviewing `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' remove tree` and removing only the package introduced for this exercise.

## Resolve another operator's claim
A colleague says the package was installed because a .rpm file exists in Downloads. Demonstrate how to answer three separate questions: what the file contains, whether the package is installed, and which installed package owns an executable.

**Check your work.** The file query uses `-p`, the installed package query uses a name, and the ownership query uses `-f` with an installed pathname. After removal the file on the DVD remains readable, but the installed database no longer reports tree.

lessons.title: Choose and verify a software source
lessons.body:
A branch office receives software over removable media. DNF needs a repository root containing `repodata/repomd.xml`. The URL refers to that root. A repository ID identifies the entry to DNF, while `name` is a human-readable label.

## Inspect a local repository
The client includes an empty practice repository. In the untimed client create `/etc/yum.repos.d/workshop.repo` with this content, then validate only that source.

```ini
[workshop]
name=Workshop shelf
baseurl=file:///srv/erudior-repo
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
```

```sh
test -r /srv/erudior-repo/repodata/repomd.xml
dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop makecache
rpm -q bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
```

Metadata refresh should succeed even though the shelf has no application packages. For a local RPM, obtain the expected signing key and its fingerprint from the trusted publisher. On a guest with the verified key in its RPM keyring run `rpmkeys --checksig --verbose ./package.rpm` on the actual file. Look for an OK signature from the expected key. Digests alone establish file integrity. Install with `sudo dnf --setopt=localpkg_gpgcheck=1 install ./package.rpm` to enforce local-file signature checks. Trusted repositories must supply any dependencies. Use `rpm -q NAME` to verify the installed version. On AlmaLinux, query the enabled sources with `dnf repolist` and update a practice package with `sudo dnf upgrade NAME` when a newer build exists. Review the transaction before removing a package you added with `sudo dnf remove NAME`.

For a network repository, obtain an approved HTTPS repository root and its key file. Create a separate [workshop-net] section with this baseurl, enabled=1, gpgcheck=1 and gpgkey pointing to the approved key. Test `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop-net makecache` and query a package available in that source.

## Self-check with a Flatpak remote
Use a guest with Flatpak and a reachable approved .flatpakrepo descriptor. Record `flatpak remotes --user --show-details` and `flatpak list --user --app`. Choose an unused remote name (training below) and an app absent from this account. Run `flatpak remote-add --user training /path/to/training.flatpakrepo` with the actual descriptor. Confirm the new URL from remote details. Run `flatpak remote-ls --user --app training`, choose a listed app and run `flatpak install --user training APP_ID`. Confirm its exact ID using `flatpak list --user --app`. Remove that ID with `flatpak uninstall --user APP_ID` and check the list again. Remove only newly installed practice refs before running `flatpak remote-delete --user training`. Keep existing apps, runtimes and remotes.

On an Internet-connected disposable guest where Flathub is approved, the remote-add step can use `flatpak remote-add --user training https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo`. A disconnected guest needs a supplied remote with accessible app and runtime content.

Without `--user`, `flatpak remote-add` and `flatpak install` act on the system-wide installation and need administrative rights. Read the task for which scope it wants, then verify with `flatpak remotes` and `flatpak list --app` (system) or the same commands with `--user`. 

On the disconnected course pair, continue to **Install from a signed Flatpak remote without Internet access** for a complete exercise with its own local source and public key.

lessons.title: Install from a signed Flatpak remote without Internet access
lessons.body:
A desktop app can be installed for just one account. Flatpak keeps that account's remotes and installed references in a different installation from the system-wide one. A remote supplies a catalog and signed objects. An application can depend on a runtime. Removing an application does not necessarily remove its runtime.

## Stock the practice shelf
On the untimed client, open **Make the offline Flatpak practice shelf** in this lesson's references. Run its setup once as learner. It creates a tiny local repository, two signed references and a public key under `~/rhcsa-flatpak-shelf`. You are acting as both publisher and consumer inside a disposable guest. The sample application contains an inventory document. The exercise assesses installation, scope and removal. For a real publisher, verify its key through a separately trusted source.

## Perform the request as the learner
First check `flatpak remotes --user` and `flatpak list --user`. Continue with an unused remote name and a fresh copy of the lab where the two exercise IDs are absent. The following commands register the shelf and inspect what it offers. Import only the **public** key.

```sh
shelf="$HOME/rhcsa-flatpak-shelf"
flatpak remote-add --user --gpg-import="$shelf/shelf.gpg" shift-shelf "file://$shelf/repo"
flatpak remote-ls --user --app shift-shelf
flatpak install --user shift-shelf org.erudior.ShelfNotes
flatpak info --user org.erudior.ShelfNotes
flatpak list --user --runtime
```

Review the proposed app and runtime during installation. If Flatpak asks where to get the runtime, choose the local shift-shelf. `flatpak info` identifies the origin. Find the payload with `flatpak info --user --show-location org.erudior.ShelfNotes` and read `files/share/inventory.txt` inside that deployment. A user installation is meaningful even on a machine without a graphical session.

## Prove removal without disturbing other software
Retire the app, its course-only runtime and this remote. In this fresh exercise use `flatpak uninstall --user org.erudior.ShelfNotes`, then `flatpak uninstall --user org.erudior.ShelfPlatform`, then `flatpak remote-delete --user shift-shelf`. Compare the before and after lists with the original baseline. Keep the shelf itself so you can repeat under a different remote name.

**Check your work.** A complete handoff shows the trusted source in the user installation, the installed app's ID and origin, the inventory text and the post-removal lists. If a colleague sees an empty list, first compare user versus system scope and the identity of the account performing the query.

lessons.title: Lab • Bring an offline RPM source online
lessons.body:
On the **client**, enable one DNF repository with the repository ID `erudior-local` (the section name in brackets) using only `file:///srv/erudior-repo` as its base URL and require RPM signature checks. The files under that directory are supplied. Complete the task with the prepared local content.

Verify that the enabled repository list shows the ID, that a metadata refresh restricted to that ID succeeds, and that its configuration sets `gpgcheck=1`. Watch for an extra `repodata` component, a duplicate section ID in another file, or a stale `mirrorlist` or `metalink`. The supplied shelf is empty, so an empty list of available packages can accompany a working configuration.

## Reason through a reported result
The shelf appears in repolist; makecache for that source alone reports that repomd.xml cannot be found. What has each test established?

**Check your reasoning.** DNF parsed an enabled entry. The second test actually tried its URL. Inspect the base directory and its repodata/repomd.xml, then refresh just that source again.

lessons.title: Tell a process, a shell job and a service apart
lessons.body:
When you launch a command, the kernel gives its process a numeric ID (PID). A shell can keep track of jobs it started. A service manager can start and supervise processes even after an administrator logs out. These are three views of running work. Killing a process belonging to a service can trigger its restart policy.

## Watch one harmless process
Start `sleep 120 &` as your regular user. The ampersand returns control of the terminal immediately. Save its PID with `worker=$!`, then run `jobs -l` and `ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,ni,comm -p "$worker"`. The parent PID identifies the process that launched it. A sleeping process usually consumes almost no CPU. Use `top`, press P to sort by CPU or M for memory, then q to exit. Compare a process's resident memory with the system view in `free -h`. Linux uses spare memory as cache; the available column includes memory it can make available to programs.

Open another terminal as the same user. Its `jobs` list does not show the first shell's job, while `ps -p PID` with the recorded number can still see it. Back in the original shell, check the PID still identifies your sleep process, then run `kill -TERM "$worker"`. Use `wait "$worker"` followed by `ps -p "$worker"` to observe completion. TERM requests termination and allows a program to clean up. Select a specific disposable process for this exercise.

**Independent ticket.** A dashboard lists two processes with the same name. Show how to distinguish them using PID, owner and parent. Before adjusting priority, decide whether the symptom is CPU contention or a process waiting for I/O. In the next exercise, predict the direction of a nice-value change before you apply it.

lessons.title: Distinguish a busy CPU from memory pressure
lessons.body:
“The server feels slow” is a symptom. Before stopping a process, find out which resource is under pressure, which process owns it and over what interval the evidence was collected. A process is one running instance of a program. Its PID distinguishes that instance from another copy with the same name.

## Read three different observations
In the client run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,stat,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`. Load averages summarize runnable work and certain waiting tasks over time. CPU utilization reports time spent doing work. In `free`, read the **available** column as well as **free**. Linux can reclaim some cached memory. Little unused RAM by itself does not prove an application needs to be killed.

Start a short-lived job you own. A background command returns the prompt. `$!` is the PID Bash recorded for that command.

```sh
sleep 300 &
job=$!
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,ni,etime,comm -p "$job"
jobs -l
renice 10 -p "$job"
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$job"
kill -TERM "$job"
wait "$job"
```

A sleeping process is normally in state S and consumes little CPU. Its parent PID identifies the shell that launched it. Increasing the numeric nice value gives other normal work more preference when the CPU is contested. It does not guarantee a percentage. A nonzero status from `wait` after a deliberate signal is expected. Recheck the saved PID immediately to see that this job has exited.

## Make a defensible incident note
Open `top`, observe two refreshes and exit with `q`. Compare the memory leader with the CPU leader using `ps` sorted separately by `-pmem` and `-pcpu`. Report PID, owner, command and sampling method. If the rankings change between samples, say so. Explain why a high CPU reading from the workload you intentionally launched would lead to a different action from the same reading on a shared service.

**Check your work.** Your report identifies an instance and an observation interval. You should be able to explain why the sleeping training process could have a large elapsed time and virtually no CPU use at the same time.

lessons.title: Follow a slowdown from process to journal
lessons.body:
A server is sluggish after a scheduled job. Start with evidence from the current boot. On the workshop server, run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,ni,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`. Reorder by `-pmem` to find memory consumers. Load, CPU use and memory pressure answer different questions. `top` shows the same ranking live; press `P` or `M` to sort, `k` to signal a process and `q` to quit. `pkill -u USER NAME` and `kill PID` send TERM by default. Use `kill -KILL` only after TERM has had a chance, because the process cannot clean up.

## Follow one process you own
```sh
nice -n 5 sleep 300 &
jobpid=$!
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$jobpid"
renice -n 10 -p "$jobpid"
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$jobpid"
kill -TERM "$jobpid"
wait "$jobpid"
```

Use a shell starting at nice value 0. The initial +5 is relative to the shell. If ps races the launch, repeat it once sleep appears. Expect nice 5, then 10 after renice. Bash wait normally returns 143 when TERM ends the sleep. A higher nice number gives a normal process a lower scheduling priority. Diagnose a service with `systemctl status NAME` and `journalctl -b -u NAME`, replacing NAME with the unit. Record the first failure and its timestamp. To preserve messages on a default journald setup using `Storage=auto`, create `/var/log/journal` with sudo, run `sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal` then `sudo journalctl --flush`. If policy explicitly sets volatile storage, configure `Storage=persistent` in a journald drop-in and restart journald. Write `logger -t workshop-boot 'workshop boot evidence'`. After a planned workshop reboot check `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t workshop-boot` or search the previous boot by message.

## Choose a tuning profile
Run `tuned-adm list`, `tuned-adm recommend` and `tuned-adm active`. Record the current profile name before changing it. On the workshop server choose an installed profile such as `balanced` with `sudo tuned-adm profile balanced`. Verify with `tuned-adm active` and `sudo tuned-adm verify`. Explain why maximizing throughput and reducing energy use can favor different settings. Restore the prior profile when finished.

lessons.title: Read a failure in the journal and preserve its evidence
lessons.body:
The first useful error often appears several lines before a final “failed” status. The journal records the unit, boot, timestamp and message. Choose the scope before drawing a conclusion. If a request failed after a reboot, the current boot may be healthy while yesterday's evidence has gone.

On your disposable system, choose a new unique name, for example `unit=shift-check-$(date +%s)`. Use `sudo systemd-run --unit="$unit" /usr/bin/false`. This asks systemd to run a temporary service whose program deliberately exits with status 1. The launcher may report that it scheduled the unit successfully. Run `sudo systemctl status "$unit.service" --no-pager` and `sudo journalctl -b -u "$unit.service" --no-pager`. Identify the executable, the exit status and the subsequent unit failure. The launch request and the program's outcome are separate events.

Compare `journalctl --list-boots`, `journalctl -b -p warning` and `sudo journalctl --since '10 minutes ago'`. Set up persistent storage and flush the journal as described in the previous workshop. Run `logger -t shift-handoff 'dispatch verified'` and look it up with `sudo journalctl -b -t shift-handoff`. Run `sudo journalctl --sync` and reboot your disposable guest. On the new boot, search `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t shift-handoff`. If boot -1 is unavailable, check the configured Storage setting and whether a persistent journal directory exists. Write a fresh marker and repeat after changing the setting.

**Independent ticket.** A manager asks for proof that the failed service ran on the *prior* boot. Supply its unit name, the earlier boot ID, one diagnostic line and its exit status. Explain why an old log line from a different boot could lead the next shift to change a healthy service.

lessons.title: Lab • Apply a persistent performance profile
lessons.body:
On the **server**, select the provided TuneD `throughput-performance` profile. The server must report that profile after startup without an interactive command.

Inspect the service state, the installed profiles and the chosen profile independently. If the name is present in the profile list but the active profile differs, determine which command selects it. If the choice vanishes after startup, examine the TuneD service and its current-boot journal. Use the grader's before/after observations to check whether your change survived.

## Reason through a reported result
The profile package exists, but tuned-adm active reports a different policy after reboot. What evidence is missing?

**Check your reasoning.** An installed profile is a choice. Verify which profile TuneD selected, that the service is running at startup, and whether the intended settings verify after boot.

lessons.title: Make a service leave evidence on every boot
lessons.body:
A service can be running now and absent after reboot. It can also be enabled and failing on every start. Use a practice oneshot unit to observe what each state means. On the workshop server save the following in `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-stamp.service`.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Record workshop startup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /run/workshop-stamp
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, then `sudo systemctl start workshop-stamp`. Compare `systemctl is-active workshop-stamp` with `systemctl is-enabled workshop-stamp`. The first should report active and the second disabled on this new unit. Now enable it with `sudo systemctl enable workshop-stamp`. Verify the marker with `stat /run/workshop-stamp`. Record `cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, run `sudo systemctl reboot` and reconnect. Confirm the boot ID changed. Inspect `stat /run/workshop-stamp` and `sudo journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`. The guest recreated /run at startup, so a marker on the new boot is evidence of a fresh invocation.

Self-check: stop the practice unit and predict both state queries before running them. Start it again and inspect `systemctl cat workshop-stamp` and `journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`. Distinguish the installed definition, systemd's loaded view and the program's actual outcome. A successful oneshot with RemainAfterExit can legitimately show `active (exited)`.

lessons.title: Repair a boot job that only root can run
lessons.body:
Dispatch receives a small boot-time job. Root can read its configuration at the console, yet systemd reports that the job failed. Your job is to explain the discrepancy, make the smallest repair, and verify the result after reboot.

Use the **untimed practice server**. The marker in this exercise is public training text. The permission fault is deliberate. Leave the practice client available for reading or notes. First check `getent passwd erushift`, `getent group erushift`, `systemctl cat erudior-shift-read.service` and `sudo ls -ld /etc/erudior-shift-read`. Start with unused names on a new pair or continue with the objects you created for this exercise.

## Install the job and observe the failure

On a fresh server, create a service identity and its configuration. The directory lets the group traverse it. The file initially allows only root to read it.

```sh
sudo groupadd --system erushift
sudo useradd --system --gid erushift --no-create-home --shell /sbin/nologin erushift
sudo install -d -o root -g erushift -m 0750 /etc/erudior-shift-read
printf '%s\n' 'shift=evening' | sudo tee /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf >/dev/null
sudo chown root:erushift /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo chmod 0600 /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/erudior-shift-read.service >/dev/null <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=Read the practice shift assignment

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=erushift
Group=erushift
ExecStart=/usr/bin/cat /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
UNIT
sudo restorecon -RF /etc/erudior-shift-read /etc/systemd/system/erudior-shift-read.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start erudior-shift-read.service
```

Expect the last command to fail. Find the denial in `sudo journalctl -b -u erudior-shift-read.service --no-pager`. Which account opened the file? Compare the unit's effective identity, the two modes and an actual read as that identity.

```sh
systemctl show erudior-shift-read.service -p User -p Group -p Result -p ExecMainStatus
namei -l /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo cat /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo -u erushift cat /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
```

The root read succeeds and the service read fails. The process needs search permission on every parent and read permission on the file. It has the former. Predict the single mode bit that will fix the latter while keeping the marker private to root and the service group.

## Repair and prove the boot result

```sh
sudo chmod g+r /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo -u erushift cat /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf
sudo -u nobody test ! -r /etc/erudior-shift-read/desk.conf && echo outsider-excluded
sudo systemctl enable --now erudior-shift-read.service
systemctl show erudior-shift-read.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus -p ActiveState
sudo journalctl -b -u erudior-shift-read.service -o cat --no-pager
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
```
