A successful oneshot can be **inactive** after completing its work. Expect Result=success, ExecMainStatus=0 and an exact shift=evening message. Earlier failures can still appear in this boot's journal. Record the boot ID and run `sudo systemctl reboot` on the practice server. Reconnect and run these checks before starting the unit yourself.

```sh
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
systemctl is-enabled erudior-shift-read.service
systemctl show erudior-shift-read.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus
sudo journalctl -b -u erudior-shift-read.service -o cat --no-pager | grep -Fx 'shift=evening'
```

## Independent repair

A second ticket arrives. Set `sudo chmod 0740 /etc/erudior-shift-read` and start the unit again. The file still has mode 0640. Show that root can read it, the configured identity cannot, and the nonzero service exit matches the journal. Repair the parent with the smallest change that restores traversal to erushift. Restart the job. Give the next operator the two final modes, the successful service result and the outsider's failed read. Award yourself the handoff only if all three are present.

To check your diagnosis, the expected modes are 0750 for the directory and 0640 for the file. Group read on a directory allows listing names. Group execute allows looking up the named file. Keep the service running as erushift and SELinux enforcing throughout.

lessons.title: Choose when a job should run and how to prove it ran
lessons.body:
A storage report is needed once after tonight’s maintenance, a second report is needed every weekday morning, and a third should catch up if the machine was off at its scheduled time. Write the three requirements as promises. The mechanism follows from the promise. An at job leaves the queue after it executes. A cron entry describes matching wall-clock minutes. A systemd calendar timer can trigger a paired service and can catch up on a missed event when Persistent=true.

Read `timedatectl` on the guest. Which time zone is in effect? A schedule for 08:00 on a server set to UTC is a different promise from 08:00 local office time. A correctly formatted date can still be wrong if the clock is drifting. Use `chronyc tracking` and `chronyc sources -v` when chronyd is installed. A selected upstream and a recent useful update are better evidence than a running process alone.

## Work it out before editing
Interpret `15 6 * * 1-5` from left to right as minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. On a normally configured cron host this matches weekdays at 06:15 in its scheduling time zone. A user's crontab has five time fields followed by its command. System crontab entries include a username field. Adding that field to a per-user crontab makes cron try to execute that word as a command.

**Independent ticket.** Put the guest's time zone, intended local time and expected next run in your notes. In the following workshop schedule a timestamp into a practice log. Find evidence at three places: the configured schedule, the scheduler's decision, and the output produced by the job. If the job works in your terminal only, compare the command's path, user, working directory and output redirection.

lessons.title: Build a scheduled service and prove it actually ran
lessons.body:
A nightly backup ticket has two separate promises: a scheduler will request work, and the work will succeed. A systemd timer represents the first. Its associated service represents the second. Checking only the next firing time leaves half the ticket untested.

## Run the work before scheduling it
Use the untimed client's **system** manager. Check `systemctl cat rhcsa-stamp.service rhcsa-stamp.timer` first. Use these names only if they are unused. In `/etc/systemd/system/rhcsa-stamp.service` create the following file with `sudoedit`.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Record a training timestamp

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/date --iso-8601=seconds
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo systemctl start rhcsa-stamp.service`. The date written to standard output goes to the journal. Inspect `journalctl -u rhcsa-stamp.service -n 8` with sudo if needed. A successful oneshot may already be inactive. `systemctl show rhcsa-stamp.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus` reports the last execution.

## Schedule it and inspect both pieces
Create `/etc/systemd/system/rhcsa-stamp.timer`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Schedule the training timestamp

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 06:15:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

The matching unit names connect the timer to the service. Validate the expression with `systemd-analyze calendar '*-*-* 06:15:00'` and read the next date in the guest's local zone. Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo systemctl enable --now rhcsa-stamp.timer`. Check `systemctl list-timers --all rhcsa-stamp.timer`. A persistent calendar timer can catch up when it becomes active after a missed firing. It does not repair a failing service.

## Deliver a schedule change
Change the timer to 17:40 on weekdays. Prove the next firing is a weekday, the timer is enabled for startup, and the underlying task still produces a timestamp. For a short live test, temporarily set `OnCalendar=minutely`, reload and restart the timer, then wait for the journal to gain a new entry without manually starting the service. Restore your weekday schedule.

**Check your work.** `Mon..Fri *-*-* 17:40:00` is one valid calendar expression. Record both the next firing and the most recent service result. To retire the exercise, disable and stop your timer, remove only these two practice unit files and reload the manager.

lessons.title: Choose a scheduler and verify its work
lessons.body:
On a disposable guest with at, cronie and chrony installed, run `sudo systemctl enable --now atd crond chronyd`. Check the guest time zone with `timedatectl`. Schedule a job that records a harmless timestamp. In an untimed guest with `at` and `atd` installed and active, run `echo '/usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-once.log' | at now + 2 minutes`. Use `atq` while waiting. The job leaves the queue after execution; check the actual log. For recurring work in an image with cronie and active crond, use `crontab -e` and add `*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-cron.log`. Confirm with `crontab -l`, wait for a matching minute, and remove only your practice line when finished. Absolute paths help when a scheduler has a smaller environment than your interactive shell.

For a systemd alternative, create `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.service` with the first block and `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.timer` with the second. The shared base name associates the timer with the service.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Write workshop journal entry
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/logger -t workshop-timer tick
```

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Run workshop log job
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* *:*:00
AccuracySec=1s
Persistent=true
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

Reload systemd, `sudo systemctl enable --now workshop-log.timer`, and inspect `systemctl list-timers --all workshop-log.timer`. After a minute read `journalctl -t workshop-timer -b`. Stop future activations and remove startup enablement with `sudo systemctl disable --now workshop-log.timer`. For a time client use `timedatectl`, `chronyc sources -v` and `chronyc tracking`. On a guest with a designated reachable NTP source, add one `server YOUR_NTP_SOURCE iburst` directive with the real address to `/etc/chrony.conf`, restart chronyd and check for a selected source (`^*`). If the time server restarted after the client, a configured source can still show ^? while the client waits for usable measurements. Check the route and the server’s NTP firewall rule on the private interface. Once the source is reachable, use `sudo chronyc online` and `sudo chronyc burst 4/4` to request fresh samples. Compare `chronyc -n sources` with `chronyc tracking` and record the selected address and reference ID. The private exam network supplies no time server. Merely starting chronyd does not prove synchronization.

lessons.title: Decide whether a server's clock can be trusted
lessons.body:
A report from two machines seems to describe events in the wrong order. The system clock represents an instant. The time zone controls how that instant is displayed. Clock synchronization disciplines the clock against a selected source. Changing the display zone can make a timestamp look familiar while leaving the two machines just as far apart.

## Read the same instant two ways
On the untimed client compare `date --iso-8601=seconds` with `date -u --iso-8601=seconds`. The zone offsets may differ. Try `TZ=America/Denver date --iso-8601=seconds`. This sets the environment for one command and leaves the machine's configured time zone untouched. On both client and server, collect:

```sh
timedatectl
systemctl is-enabled chronyd
systemctl is-active chronyd
chronyc sources -v
chronyc tracking
```

A running daemon can still lack a usable time source. In the source list, `^` identifies a server source and `*` marks the selected source. A `?` indicates an unusable or as-yet-unmeasured source. Check reachability, synchronization state and elapsed time since startup. On an isolated lab, an unreachable Internet pool is a valid observation. It does not establish synchronization. Use UTC when comparing journal entries across machines.

## Configure a client against a supplied source
On the practice client, first establish the address of an approved reachable NTP server. For an offline pair, use the local chrony server setup in **Build your own client and server**. Verify the server allows the lab subnet and its firewall permits the NTP service there. Keep a copy of the client's `/etc/chrony.conf`. Add a single `server 192.168.77.10 iburst` directive when .10 is that prepared source. Restart `chronyd`, wait for polling and compare `chronyc sources -n` with `chronyc tracking`. If several sources are usable, chrony may select a different one. Report what the selection marker says. Restore your original configuration after the exercise.

## Decide whether to close the ticket
One guest reports `active` and all sources `^?`. The other reports a selected source and a recent reference time. Which evidence would you request before claiming the first system has reliable time? Translate a journal record to UTC and compare it against the other guest.

**Check your work.** Give the source address, selection state, reach field and last reference time, plus one timestamp from `journalctl --utc -n 1`. A private server using chrony's local reference is useful for practicing the protocol. It does not establish the accuracy of that server's clock against an external standard.

lessons.title: Lab • Restore a startup service
lessons.body:
On the **server**, the supplied `erudior-maint.service` creates a runtime marker. Start it now and enable it for future boots. Inspect the supplied unit before you change its state.

Use two systemctl queries to verify active and enabled independently. Then inspect `/run/erudior-maint.ready` and the unit's journal. If it is active but disabled, decide what the next reboot would do. If it is enabled but failed, read the first error in the current boot. Leave the supplied unit performing its original job and submit for the reboot check.

## Reason through a reported result
Immediately after enabling a unit it still reports inactive. How can both observations be true?

**Check your reasoning.** Enablement connects the unit to a future startup target. Inspect the live status and use the expected runtime marker to distinguish starting now from enabling for boot.

lessons.title: Lab • Schedule a recurring job
lessons.body:
On the **client**, add an entry to the `learner` account's own crontab that runs `logger erudior-nightly` every day at 02:15.

Edit as that user with `crontab -e`, or as root with `crontab -e -u learner`. The five time fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. Confirm the entry with `crontab -l -u learner` and that `crond` is active and enabled. A one-time test is to add a second entry for the next minute, watch `journalctl -t learner -f` or `journalctl -f | grep erudior`, then remove the test line.

The grader reads learner's crontab and checks the daily 02:15 entry and the daemon, before and after a client reboot. Entries in `/etc/crontab` or `/etc/cron.d` do not count for this task, because it asks for the user's own table.

lessons.title: Independent shift: diagnose a service that missed its schedule
lessons.body:
A branch office wants an audit timestamp once per hour. Another operator enabled a timer, saw a next run, and marked the request complete. The handoff folder is empty. Your job is to reproduce the failure, narrow it to one layer, repair it and leave evidence that the next operator can repeat. Use a disposable untimed client with the timer workshop completed or use fresh unit names.

## Build the incident on your training client
Using the paired-unit design from the timer workshop, create `rhcsa-audit.service` and `rhcsa-audit.timer`. Use `OnCalendar=hourly` for the timer and `WantedBy=timers.target`. In the oneshot service use `ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /run/rhcsa-shift-audit/delivered`. Start with `/run/rhcsa-shift-audit` absent and ensure both names are unused. Set up and enable the timer. Trigger the service manually once to gather evidence now. Write down the exact command that failed and the relevant journal message.

## Repair the actual cause
The configuration must recreate its required runtime directory on every service activation, leave the marker visible after a successful run, and schedule future work across boot. The filesystem under `/run` is temporary. Creating the directory manually once can hide the defect until the next boot. Find a service configuration or a preparation action that meets these conditions. Avoid changing unrelated permissions on /run.

Award one check each for a recorded initial failure, a successful manual service run, an enabled timer with a plausible next firing, and a repeated successful trigger after reboot. Wait for both practice machines to return. Record the new boot ID. A missing marker immediately after boot is expected if no scheduled activation has occurred yet. Prove what happens when the service actually runs.

## Worked review
One solution adds `ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/mkdir -p /run/rhcsa-shift-audit` in the service's `[Service]` section. The manager runs it before the existing `ExecStart`. Reload the units, start the service and compare the marker's modification time with the journal. Review `systemctl show rhcsa-audit.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus`. Query `is-enabled` and `list-timers` for the timer. Repeat after reboot. Disable and stop the training timer and remove only its two practice units when you finish.

lessons.title: Build a decision from arguments and exit statuses
lessons.body:
A script is a saved series of shell instructions. Its caller needs to know what to pass in, what output to expect and how failure is reported. Start with an ordinary task: label a shipment as small or bulk. For this exercise enter one to four ASCII digits for a package count between 0 and 9999. Leading zeroes are allowed. Writing down the contract lets you decide what to do with 9, 10, an empty input and the word ten.

Save the following in a fresh file called shipment. Use your editor, then inspect the first line before running it.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo 'give one package count' >&2
    exit 2
fi
case "$1" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*|?????*) echo 'use one to four digits' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
if [ "$1" -lt 10 ]; then
    echo small
else
    echo bulk
fi
```

The first line selects the interpreter. The shell supplies the number of arguments in `$#` and the first argument in `$1`. The test command inside brackets returns an exit status that if uses to choose a branch. Leave spaces around its words. Run `chmod u+x shipment`. Then run `./shipment 9`, `./shipment 10`, `./shipment 0009`, `./shipment 9999`, `./shipment 10000`, `./shipment ten` and `./shipment`. Inspect `echo $?` directly after each. The invalid cases should write a diagnostic and exit 2. The threshold itself belongs in the upper group.

**Independent ticket.** Change the boundary to 25 and process three separate counts without editing the script again. Try `for count in 24 25 26; do ./shipment "$count"; done`. Explain what varies on each iteration and what stays fixed. In the next workshop you will preserve multiple input filenames, including names with spaces, and capture the output of another command inside the script.

lessons.title: Turn a shell command into a testable tool
lessons.body:
The next shift needs a tool that can report on several files without losing a filename that contains spaces. A script has a contract. Specify its arguments, output, exit status and required permissions before you write it.

In your home directory, save this as `line-report`. The first line selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly. Quotes around `"$@"` preserve the original arguments individually.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' 'supply at least one file' >&2
    exit 2
fi
for file in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$file" ] && [ -r "$file" ]; then
        lines=$(wc -l < "$file") || exit 1
        printf '%s %s\n' "$lines" "$file"
    else
        printf 'unreadable: %s\n' "$file" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
done
```

Run `chmod 755 line-report`. Create a file containing two newline-terminated lines named `shift notes`. Run `./line-report 'shift notes'` and check for `2 shift notes`. Run `./line-report missing >out.txt 2>err.txt`, immediately check `echo $?`, and inspect both files. An error belongs on standard error so the next program can use standard output as data.

## Try a numeric boundary
Make a second executable that reads its first argument as a number and prints `low` below 5 and `high` otherwise. Use the shell numeric test `[ "$1" -lt 5 ]`, leaving spaces around the bracket tokens. Exercise 0, 4, 5 and 17. Try launching the installed script by its full path as a second user. A script that works only when invoked with `bash scriptname` may have a bad shebang or lack execute permission.

lessons.title: Write a read-only inventory script and test its contract
lessons.body:
Night shift needs a list of the files that exist and the paths that were missing. An operator must be able to pass several paths, including one with a space, and use the exit status in a second script. Start by specifying what success and failure mean. A command can print something plausible while still handling an edge case incorrectly.

## Build one small program
Create a fresh directory in the learner's home or a new temporary directory. Open a file called `inventory` in your editor and enter this complete script. The first line chooses Bash. `"$@"` expands to one argument per input, preserving the original boundaries.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf 'usage: inventory PATH ...\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
result=0
for path in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$path" ]; then
        bytes=$(wc -c < "$path") || exit 1
        printf '%s bytes\t%s\n' "$bytes" "$path"
    else
        printf 'not a regular file: %s\n' "$path" >&2
        result=1
    fi
done
exit "$result"
```

Run `bash -n inventory` to check syntax. Set owner execute permission with `chmod u+x inventory`. Use `printf 'abc' > 'day one'`. The absence of a trailing newline makes the expected size three bytes. Run `./inventory 'day one' missing >good 2>problems` and immediately save `rc=$?`. Read the two files, then print the saved status. The valid file still appears despite the missing argument. A nonzero status carries the partial failure back to the caller.

## Change a requirement
Make a zero-length regular file and a directory whose name contains a space. Run the script with each alone, both together and no arguments. Build a table of input, output stream and exit status **before** running them. Finally modify a copy of the script to count successful regular files and print a summary, including when there are zero. Keep its exit-status contract.

**Check your work.** An empty regular file is valid with a byte count of zero. A directory produces a diagnostic and status 1. No arguments produces usage and status 2. Mixed inputs produce evidence for both cases. Swapping the argument order must preserve the overall failure. Explain why setting result back to zero on each later success would introduce a bug.

lessons.title: Lab • Deliver an executable classifier
lessons.body:
On the **client**, install `/usr/local/bin/lab-classify` as an executable shell script for an unprivileged user. Given one nonnegative integer, it must print exactly `small` below 10 and `large` for 10 or higher. The command should run directly by absolute path.

Write your own tests first. Include 0, 9, 10 and a larger value you choose. Run them as `learner` and compare the exact standard output. If a root-run test works and a learner test fails, inspect the shebang, directory traversal and file mode. Extra prompts or debug output on stdout change the result.

## Reason through a reported result
Running sh /usr/local/bin/lab-classify 10 prints large; executing the file by its full path as learner returns Permission denied. Which part of the contract failed?

**Check your reasoning.** Calling sh reads the script as input and bypasses the direct-execution check. Inspect execute permission and ancestor traversal, then test the full path as learner.

lessons.title: Trace a file down to the disk that holds it
lessons.body:
A directory is a location in the names you can walk through. A filesystem is the structure that stores names, data and metadata. A mount attaches the root of a filesystem at a directory. A partition is a bounded region of a disk. LVM adds another layer that lets logical volumes draw from a shared pool of storage. The size of a disk, a logical volume and a mounted filesystem can legitimately differ.

## Work backwards from a file
Run `findmnt -T /etc/hosts` on your VM. Read SOURCE, TARGET and FSTYPE. Use `lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS` to follow the mount's source toward a disk. On a machine using LVM it may go through a logical volume and a partition. On a simpler installation the filesystem can occupy a partition directly. Compare `df -hT /` with `du -sh ~/shift-practice` if that directory exists. The first reports capacity of the containing filesystem. The second totals a particular directory tree.

**Read this case.** A guest has a 20 GiB virtual disk. One partition occupies 12 GiB and its volume group has 4 GiB free. A mounted XFS logical volume of 5 GiB is full. If you need 1 GiB more there, allocating a new virtual disk is unnecessary. Check free extents in `vgs`, enlarge the correct logical volume, grow the filesystem, then verify the mount gained capacity. Equality between `lsblk` disk size and `df` space would be the wrong success criterion.

## Identify a new practice disk
On a manual VM record your current `lsblk` tree. Power it off, attach one new, empty 2 GiB virtual disk and boot it. Identify the added device by the before/after inventory, size, mountpoints, children and any filesystem signatures. Run `sudo wipefs --no-act DEVICE` with the newly identified path to inspect signatures without changing it. If you cannot distinguish the data disk from the boot disk, use the new temporary file and loop procedure in the next lesson.

**Independent ticket.** Draw the actual layers serving / on your machine. Circle the layer where unused space would need to exist before you could extend an existing LV. Keep a copy of this inventory for comparison after your storage workshop.

lessons.title: Draw a partition table before changing a disk
lessons.body:
A disk is a sequence of addressable blocks. GPT is a table that describes which ranges belong to partitions. An empty partition still needs a consumer, such as a filesystem, swap or an LVM physical volume. A mountpoint is a directory in the running system. Knowing a directory's name does not identify which disk you are about to change.

## Provision a miniature disk inside the client
Use the ordinary learner account in the disposable practice guest. This exercise uses a newly created file as a disk, so your system disk and the course's extra disks can stay attached. Install `parted` from the trusted DVD if it is absent. Have 160 MiB of space available. Keep the same terminal open so the variables remain available.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
truncate -s 160M "$work/training.img"
loop=$(sudo losetup --find --show --partscan "$work/training.img")
sudo losetup -l "$loop"
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS "$loop"
```

Stop until the reported backing path is exactly your new `training.img` and there are no mounts on that loop device. The next command writes a new partition table. Use only this verified loop device. A MiB is 1,048,576 bytes. Starting at 1 MiB leaves space for the table and aligns the partition.

```sh
sudo parted -s "$loop" mklabel gpt mkpart reports 1MiB 65MiB
sudo partprobe "$loop"
sudo udevadm settle
sudo parted -s "$loop" unit MiB print free
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE "$loop"
```

The first partition is about 64 MiB. It has no filesystem yet. Free space remains after it. Predict where a second 48 MiB partition could fit without changing the start or end of the first. Create it using `sudo parted -s "$loop" mkpart later 65MiB 113MiB`. Reread the table and check both ranges. A GPT partition name identifies a table entry; a filesystem label is written by a filesystem tool inside that entry.

## Reverse one change
Remove only the second partition on this new loop disk. Prove the first partition's number, start and end are unchanged and the old second range is free again. Then detach the loop device. The backing file keeps the partition table. Reattaching with `--partscan` lets you inspect it again.

**Check your work.** On this two-partition practice table, `sudo parted -s "$loop" rm 2` removes entry 2. After `partprobe`, `udevadm settle` and `print free`, entry 1 still spans 1–65 MiB. Use `sudo losetup -d "$loop"` after verifying that neither partition is mounted. In the following LVM workshop you will build a different, larger disk and follow its layers all the way to a file.

lessons.title: Build and extend a disposable LVM volume
lessons.body:
A department needs a filesystem that can grow without moving its existing data. A partition can hold an LVM physical volume (PV). A volume group (VG) pools capacity. A logical volume (LV) draws space from the pool. Growing the LV and growing the filesystem are distinct operations.

## Self-check using a new file as a practice disk
Use a disposable AlmaLinux 10 guest with loop devices, parted, LVM2 and XFS tools. Run the blocks in the same root shell (`sudo -i`). Use only the newly allocated loop device reported below. Stop if `vgs workshp_vg` already finds a group with that name, or `/mnt/workshp_lv` is already in use. This exercise needs about 1 GiB of free space. The regular-file disk lets you practice without repartitioning a system disk.

```sh
diskfile=$(mktemp /var/tmp/rhcsa-disk.XXXXXX)
truncate -s 1G "$diskfile"
loop=$(losetup --find --show --partscan "$diskfile")
losetup "$loop"
parted -s "$loop" mklabel gpt mkpart primary 1MiB 100%
partprobe "$loop"
udevadm settle
part="$loop"p1
lsblk -o PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE "$loop"
```

Confirm the partition path shown by `lsblk` equals `$part`. If the LVM devices file is in use and the partition is not visible to LVM, add only the practice partition with `lvmdevices --adddev "$part"`. An image filtering loop devices may require an attached unused training disk instead. Do not substitute the boot disk.

```sh
pvcreate "$part"
vgcreate workshp_vg "$part"
lvcreate -L 400M -n reports workshp_vg
mkfs.xfs /dev/workshp_vg/reports
mkdir /mnt/workshp_lv
mount /dev/workshp_vg/reports /mnt/workshp_lv
printf 'keep me\n' > /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvextend -L +128M -r /dev/workshp_vg/reports
cat /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvs
```

Expect more space and unchanged proof text. `-r` requests a matching filesystem resize. Use `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` to find which layer lacks space if growth fails. A loop mapping lasts only for this exercise. Practice mounting by UUID across reboot on an attached practice disk in the next module.

## Clean up the disk you created
After confirming `losetup "$loop"` still shows your temporary file and `findmnt /mnt/workshp_lv` identifies your practice LV, unmount it. Remove the practice LV, then the VG, then its PV label using `lvremove /dev/workshp_vg/reports`, `vgremove workshp_vg` and `pvremove "$part"`. If you added the partition to the LVM devices file, remove its entry if still present. Delete partition 1 on that loop disk with `parted -s "$loop" rm 1`, detach with `losetup -d "$loop"`, then remove your temporary file and empty mount directory. Check `lvs` and `losetup -j "$diskfile"` to confirm retirement.

lessons.title: Activate swap and make it return at startup
lessons.body:
Swap supplies extra backing space for idle memory pages. An allocated file, a swap signature, activation now and a boot-time entry are four distinct states. On the untimed server inspect `free -h`, `swapon --show --bytes`, `df -h /var/lib` and `findmnt -T /var/lib`. Use the following on the workshop guest's local XFS or ext4 filesystem. Choose a fresh path and ensure at least 70 MiB is free.

```sh
sudo sh -c 'set -C; umask 077; dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=65 status=none > /var/lib/workshop.swap'
```

If creation failed or the path already existed, stop and choose a new path. Inspect the resulting regular file and mode with `sudo stat /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Initialize your new file with `sudo mkswap /var/lib/workshop.swap` and activate it with `sudo swapon /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Verify the name and size with `swapon --show --bytes`. Allocating real blocks avoids sparse-file activation errors.

Edit `/etc/fstab` and add one line `/var/lib/workshop.swap none swap defaults 0 0` after confirming that path has no existing entry. Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo findmnt --verify`. Reboot the untimed guest and run `swapon --show` again. A clean configuration file alone cannot prove that the kernel activated the space.

## Swap on a new partition or logical volume
Tasks often ask for swap on new block storage instead of a file. On a disposable guest with an attached practice disk, create a partition with `parted` (type it `linux-swap` with `mkpart swap linux-swap 1MiB 513MiB`) or a new LV with `lvcreate -L 512M -n swap2 VG`. Leave existing partitions and volumes untouched. Run `mkswap` on the new device and note the UUID it prints. Add a line such as `UUID=actual-uuid none swap defaults 0 0`, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo swapon -a`. Confirm the new device in `swapon --show` before and after a reboot. A swap device has no mountpoint, so its fstab line uses `none` and the type `swap`.

lessons.title: Add capacity without disturbing existing data
lessons.body:
A branch can attach a second disk but cannot take the archive offline. A volume group can combine physical volumes so an existing logical volume can grow. The existing filesystem keeps its identity. Your job is to prove both that the data survived and that the new capacity reached the application.

On a disposable manual VM, attach two fresh virtual disks of 2 GiB each. Take an inventory before and after, then work only on these confirmed empty disks. Use the GPT and LVM workshop procedure on the first disk to make a VG named branchtest and a 512 MiB LV called inbox. Give it ext4 with `mkfs.ext4`, mount it at /mnt/branchtest and create a file containing a handoff note. Record its checksum and `df -B1 /mnt/branchtest`. Leave existing system partitions and VGs alone.

Use `sudo parted DEVICE print` to identify the second disposable disk, replacing DEVICE with its verified path. A blank disk can report an unrecognized disk label. Following the partitioning procedure in the LVM workshop, create a GPT with one partition, settle device discovery and inspect the new partition path. In the commands below set `newpart` to that actual partition. On a host using the LVM devices file, add that practice partition to the devices file if necessary.

```sh
sudo pvcreate "$newpart"
sudo vgextend branchtest "$newpart"
sudo pvs -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_free
sudo lvextend -L +256M /dev/branchtest/inbox "$newpart"
sudo resize2fs /dev/branchtest/inbox
df -hT /mnt/branchtest
```

The LV grows first. resize2fs expands the mounted ext4 filesystem to use the larger device. An XFS filesystem instead grows online through its mountpoint with xfs_growfs. The earlier workshop used lvextend -r to request both operations together. Read the note again and compare its checksum. A larger LV with an unchanged filesystem size is unfinished work.

**Independent ticket.** Report the new PV, the VG's remaining free space, the larger filesystem and the matching checksum. Use the mount-by-UUID exercise to add persistence on your clone. For cleanup, remove any practice fstab entry, reload systemd, unmount your test filesystem, and retire the LV, VG and both PV labels only after identifying each against your recorded inventory. Remove your test disks in the hypervisor only when the clone no longer depends on them.

lessons.title: Lab • Add persistent swap capacity
lessons.body:
On the **server**, add an active swap file at `/var/lib/erudior.swap` with at least 64 MiB of file allocation and make it activate automatically at boot. Leave existing swap and filesystem entries intact. Use a 65 MiB file in this exercise. The kernel reserves a header, so swapon reports slightly less usable space than the file length.

Use `swapon --show --bytes` to confirm the path and usable size. Check that the regular file is private to root, its entry appears once in `/etc/fstab`, and the file is fully allocated. If the grader sees the file now but loses it after boot, inspect the boot-time configuration and swap unit journal.

## Reason through a reported result
The swap file is 65 MiB and was present after reboot, yet swapon --show lists only the original device. Has the new swap helped?

**Check your reasoning.** Its file survived, but the kernel has not activated it. Check the exact fstab path and swap type, verify configuration and repeat the activation check.

lessons.title: Lab • Build persistent storage on a new disk
lessons.body:
Use the dedicated empty 2 GiB grading disk at `/dev/disk/by-id/virtio-erudior-data`. Confirm its serial number with `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,SERIAL,MOUNTPOINTS`. The practice kit also supplies other 2 GiB disks. Find it before you change anything: `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINTS` lists the system disk with mounted partitions and the empty one without. Its stable name is `/dev/disk/by-id/virtio-erudior-data`. Every change in this lab goes on that disk only.

On the **server**:

1. Create volume group `labvg` with a 400 MiB logical volume `labdata`. Format it with XFS and mount it at `/srv/labdata` so it returns after boot.
2. Add at least 256 MiB of swap on the same disk, as a partition or a second logical volume, and make it activate after boot. Keep the existing swap.

Plan the disk first. One way is a GPT label with two partitions: one for LVM and one for swap. Another is one partition for LVM holding both logical volumes. Use `parted` (`mklabel gpt`, `mkpart`, `set N lvm on`), then `pvcreate`, `vgcreate`, `lvcreate`, `mkfs.xfs` and `mkswap`. Reference the filesystem and the swap device in `/etc/fstab` by UUID, run `systemctl daemon-reload`, then `mount -a` and `swapon -a` to test the entries before the grader reboots the server.

The grader checks the volume group, the logical volume's size (allowing for extent rounding), XFS mounted at the path, swap of the requested size on this disk, and all of it again after a reboot. `findmnt --verify` catches most fstab typing errors.

lessons.title: Explain why a file disappears under a mount
lessons.body:
A colleague remembers putting handoff.txt in /mnt/dispatch. You see an empty directory at that location. Before deciding anyone deleted data, ask which filesystem currently supplies the path. A mount can cover files in an existing directory. Unmounting exposes them again.

On a disposable guest pick a fresh directory under your home with `work=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/mount-practice.XXXXXX")`. Save the original marker with `printf 'underneath\n' > "$work/handoff.txt"`. Record `findmnt -T "$work"`. Mount a small temporary memory filesystem with `sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=8m tmpfs "$work"` and inspect `findmnt -T "$work"` and `ls -la "$work"` again. The first marker seems to have vanished. Add a different marker with `echo visible | sudo tee "$work/live.txt"`. Before unmounting, predict which marker will remain.

From outside the mounted directory, run `sudo umount "$work"`, then `ls -la "$work"` and `cat "$work/handoff.txt"`. This new listing comes from the original filesystem. The temporary filesystem is gone. Remove your original marker and the empty temporary directory when finished. If a real unmount says busy, first check whether a shell is using the mount as its working directory.

**Independent ticket.** A backup job wrote 200 MiB into a directory before the data disk mounted. After the mount, the files disappear and space on the root filesystem stays low. Draw the two storage locations. State which source you would verify before moving any data. In the next workshop, use a marker, a UUID and a reboot to prove which filesystem serves a path.

lessons.title: Prove which filesystem contains a user's report
lessons.body:
A newly mounted empty filesystem can make an existing directory appear empty. The files previously visible there still belong to the filesystem underneath it. If an operator writes a new report before the intended filesystem is mounted, it may disappear from view after the mount returns. Use a small temporary filesystem to see both sides of this problem.

## Observe one pathname backed by two sources
On the untimed client, create a new directory. Capture its current source and filesystem type before mounting anything on it.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir "$work/reports"
printf 'underlying disk\n' > "$work/reports/before"
findmnt -T "$work/reports/before" -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=4M,mode=0755 tmpfs "$work/reports"
ls -la "$work/reports"
findmnt -T "$work/reports" -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
```

The name `before` is now hidden. The mount changed what path resolution reaches when it enters `reports`. `tmpfs` stores its files in memory-backed storage. It is a useful stand-in for a second filesystem because the mount starts empty. Create evidence **inside** the mount with `printf 'temporary view\n' | sudo tee "$work/reports/during"`. Record the source for that file and check the original marker is absent.

## Reverse it and explain the ticket
From outside the mount, run `sudo umount "$work/reports"`. List the directory again and run `findmnt -T "$work/reports/before"`. Predict which file will be visible. This tmpfs loses its contents when its last mount is removed. A disk-backed filesystem would retain its data on that disk.

**Check your work.** `before` is back and `during` is gone from the pathname. Write a brief response to a user who copied a file during an NFS outage and can no longer see it once NFS returns. Explain how you would inspect each backing filesystem on a practice system without deleting or overwriting either copy. For a real persistent mount, add the device UUID, expected type and a post-reboot file check to your handoff.

lessons.title: Mount the right filesystem and prove what is serving a path
lessons.body:
On the server inspect `lsblk -f`, `findmnt -T /` and `sudo blkid`. Device names can change after hardware changes. A filesystem UUID or unique label identifies the intended filesystem across boots. A mounted filesystem also hides whatever was in the mount directory underneath it.

## Self-check with disposable filesystems
Use the new-file and loop procedure in **Build and extend a disposable LVM volume** on a disposable guest, with a fresh backing file for each filesystem. For each new empty partition, choose **one** formatter: `mkfs.ext4 -L TRAINEXT "$part"`, `mkfs.xfs -L TRAINXFS "$part"`, or `mkfs.vfat -n TRAINVF "$part"`. VFAT needs dosfstools. Never reformat a partition whose data you intend to keep. Create an empty practice mountpoint, mount the partition, write and read a marker, and use `findmnt -T /path/to/marker` to record the source and type. Unmount, verify the marker disappears, remount and verify it returns. VFAT generally expresses ownership and masks through mount options.

For a boot test, use a persistent, attached practice disk. Mount its filesystem by UUID or by LABEL at a new path. For example, with an ext4 volume add a single `UUID=actual-uuid /mnt/reports ext4 defaults 0 2` line to `/etc/fstab`, using the real identifier from `blkid`. Create the mountpoint, unmount any manual mount, reload systemd, run `sudo findmnt --verify` and `sudo mount /mnt/reports`. Verify the source and marker after a reboot. Remove the entry before retiring the disk.

## Self-check the network path
In the untimed client, mount the supplied server export once at a separate empty location. Run `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-check`, `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-check` and inspect the marker with `findmnt -T /mnt/nfs-check/erudior-lab.txt`. Unmount this test with `sudo umount /mnt/nfs-check`. Compare that manual mount with the direct map in the following NFS workshop. Autofs installs a trigger; reading a path makes the NFS mount appear. A local directory with a copied file cannot supply the live server's data.

lessons.title: Build a manual NFS client before automating access
lessons.body:
Network File System (NFS) lets a client access data another machine exports. There are two names for every shared file in this exercise. The server stores it under /srv/projects. The client will see the same bytes through a mount at a different path. Creating a local directory with a similar name cannot make it follow server changes.

On the prepared server run `sudo exportfs -v` and read the allowed client and access options. On the client create an empty directory, for example `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-observe`. Mount the share with `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-observe`. Run `findmnt -T /mnt/nfs-observe/erudior-lab.txt` and read the marker. Confirm that the source includes the server and export and the type is nfs or nfs4. Change out of the mounted path before running `sudo umount /mnt/nfs-observe`.

## Replace eager mounting with a trigger
A direct autofs map maps an absolute client pathname to a server export. The master file points to the map, autofs watches the trigger, and opening a file inside that path causes the actual NFS mount. In **Workshop: trigger a network mount from the client**, configure the two short map files. Before touching the path, examine `findmnt -t autofs`. After reading the marker, examine `findmnt -t nfs,nfs4`. The two listings show different stages of the request. The NFS mount can expire after inactivity while autofs keeps waiting.

**Independent ticket.** A client has the correct marker text but the source is its local root filesystem. Explain how someone could get a misleading success. On the server add a fresh marker to the same export. Read it under the client path and identify the network mount that supplied it. If manual mounting fails, investigate the export and connectivity first. If only on-demand access fails, investigate the map key, file suffix and the autofs journal.

lessons.title: Workshop: trigger a network mount from the client
lessons.body:
This dedicated two-machine workshop gives you a separate attempt to configure an on-demand NFS mount. Use **Start lab** in this lesson and log in to each console in turn. First check the server export and a manual client mount as you practiced in the preceding reading. **Check my work** verifies the on-demand mount in this workshop. Use the shared practice terminal in ordinary readings for your other experiments.

## Trace a request between the guests
On the server, run `sudo exportfs -v` and `cat /srv/projects/erudior-lab.txt`. Note the allowed client and the first few characters of the file. On the client, run `ip route get 192.168.77.10`. Look for the outgoing interface and source address. Confirm both guests' addresses before editing.

## Make one mount work
On the client, create `/etc/auto.master.d/workshop.autofs` containing the first line below. Create `/etc/auto.workshop` containing the second line. Each file has one line. A direct map uses a full client path as its key.

```text
/- /etc/auto.workshop
/mnt/projects -fstype=nfs,ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects
```

Run `sudo systemctl enable --now autofs` and `sudo systemctl reload autofs`. Then run `cat /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` and `findmnt -T /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` on the client. Expect the same marker as on the server and an NFS filesystem. A missing path calls for checking the master file's `.autofs` suffix, the map key and the service journal.

Choose **Check my work** when ready. It reboots the client and checks again. Read the before/after observations. Reopen this lesson for future walkthroughs and keep your own evidence in a notebook. In later graded labs, keep working until you have checked the requested state, then choose **Submit exam**.

lessons.title: Lab • Recover a share on demand
lessons.body:
On the **client**, configure autofs for the read-only server export `192.168.77.10:/srv/projects` at `/mnt/projects`. The application must be able to open `/mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` on demand, including after the client restarts.

Start by reading the marker at its source on the server. On the client check the master map include, your direct-map key, and the autofs service state. Trigger the mount by opening the marker. Inspect the exact file with `findmnt -T /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt`. If the client can mount the export manually at another empty directory but the application path fails, inspect your autofs maps and `journalctl -b -u autofs`. Submit to check the post-reboot behavior.

## Reason through a reported result
A marker can be read after reboot, but findmnt for it reports the root XFS volume. Does the share work?

**Check your reasoning.** The client read local data. Verify the map key and trigger, then inspect the exact marker path for a remote source.

lessons.title: Read the running kernel and the next boot entry
lessons.body:
A kernel update can be installed while the machine continues running the previous kernel. There are three separate questions: which kernel packages are on disk, which kernel booted this guest, and which entry is selected by default for a future boot. Conflating them turns a routine update into a confusing incident report.

## Follow the boot chain
Firmware selects a boot device. The bootloader selects an entry containing a kernel, an initial RAM filesystem and arguments. The kernel and early userspace make the real root filesystem available. The system manager starts the selected target and its dependencies. A missing root device, an invalid optional mount, and a failing application service occur at different points in that sequence.

On the running untimed client, compare the commands below. `grubby` and the boot files live inside the guest. Use the guest console for the subsequent boot labs.

```sh
uname -r
rpm -q kernel-core
sudo grubby --default-kernel
sudo grubby --info=DEFAULT
cat /proc/cmdline
systemctl get-default
```

Find the version in the default kernel path. Compare it with `uname -r` and the RPM list. All three can agree on a newly installed guest. If multiple kernels exist, the current version and next default can differ. `/proc/cmdline` reports what this boot actually received. The systemd default target tells you which collection of units the manager should start in its normal configuration. It does not select a kernel.

## Make a boot handoff
An operator claims the latest installed kernel is already running because the package manager listed it. Collect a short handoff answering all three questions. Then record one argument from the current command line and look for it in the selected boot entry. A one-time menu edit may explain a difference. In the following boot-target lesson, test a temporary argument and confirm the normal selection returns on the next startup.

**Check your work.** Your handoff gives a running release, the installed package version or versions and an explicit default boot path. If they match, report that observation. If they differ, identify the next evidence you need before changing any default. Keep an existing working entry available during boot practice.

lessons.title: Practice a one-time boot change and restore normal startup
lessons.body:
Use a disposable clone with a working console and a known root password for rescue-mode authentication. On your own clone with a locked root account, an authorized sudo administrator can set a temporary root password before the exercise with `sudo passwd root`.

In the untimed server, run `systemctl get-default`, `systemctl list-units --type=target --state=active` and `cat /proc/cmdline`. The configured default is the goal for a normal startup. The running boot can have reached several targets at once.

## Self-check at a local VM console
Use a disposable AlmaLinux 10 guest with a visible bootloader console and known authorized administrative credentials for rescue mode. Some cloud images lock the root account or hide the early boot menu. Use a suitable console-equipped practice image for this exercise. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel, press `e`, append `systemd.unit=rescue.target` to the kernel command line, and use the on-screen boot key (usually Ctrl+x). Authenticate when prompted. Run `cat /proc/cmdline` and `systemctl is-active rescue.target`. Resume normal service with `systemctl default`. Reboot normally and confirm the one-time kernel argument has disappeared. For a headless server, practice configuring `multi-user.target` as the default with `sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target`. Verify with `systemctl get-default`. Restore the original default when finished.

On an AlmaLinux guest with `grubby`, inspect `sudo grubby --info=DEFAULT`. Practice a reversible persistent change to the default kernel entry: save its path using `kernel=$(sudo grubby --default-kernel)`, and record the path outside the VM. Use an entry whose args contain no existing systemd.show_status setting. Add an informational argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, then inspect the entry. After booting that entry, check `/proc/cmdline`. Remove only your added argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --remove-args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, reselecting the saved path if you logged in anew. Start and stop guests cleanly with `sudo systemctl reboot` and `sudo systemctl poweroff` in a disposable console exercise.

lessons.title: Repair a failed mount from the guest console
lessons.body:
At power-on the firmware starts the bootloader, which loads a kernel and an initial RAM filesystem. That early environment finds the real root filesystem. The kernel starts systemd, which brings up the configured target and its units. A misspelled data-volume UUID is a useful diagnostic case: the kernel may boot normally while a later mount fails.

## Rehearse recovery on a disposable clone
Use a powered-off snapshot of a VM you administer, with a working hypervisor console and a known root password for rescue login. If the root account is locked on your own clone, an authorized sudo administrator can set a temporary root password there with `sudo passwd root` before the drill. Keep this clone separate from the timed guests. Save a known-good copy with `sudo cp -p /etc/fstab /root/fstab.before-drill`. Run `systemctl get-default` and `findmnt -T /` and record both.

Create /mnt/drill on the clone and add the following line to /etc/fstab in an editor. The label intentionally names a nonexistent practice filesystem. The noauto flag keeps it out of the normal startup transaction.

```text
LABEL=ABSENTDRILL /mnt/drill ext4 noauto 0 0
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and request the mount explicitly with `sudo mount /mnt/drill`. Read the diagnostic and compare the label with `lsblk -f`. The declared identity cannot be resolved. At the guest console reboot and use the preceding lesson's one-boot rescue target. Authenticate, compare the active target and the saved default, and fix only the added line with your editor. You can check your work against /root/fstab.before-drill using diff. Run `systemctl daemon-reload` and `findmnt --verify`. Return to normal service, reboot, and verify the recorded default and root mount. A preexisting warning needs separate interpretation; your practice error should be gone.

**Independent ticket.** Explain at which boot stage your practice definition would matter if it were required automatically. Show how you would distinguish a missing device from a wrong filesystem type, using its signature and an observed error. The exercise leaves ordinary boot available even if you need more time to finish.

lessons.title: Recover root access by interrupting the boot
lessons.body:
A server's root password has been lost and no account with sudo remains. With console access you can stop the boot early, set a new password and let SELinux repair the changed file's label. Practice only on a disposable RHEL 10 guest whose boot menu you can reach and whose disk is not encrypted. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

## Reset the password from an early shell
At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel and press `e`. On the line that starts with `linux`, remove `rhgb quiet` so messages stay visible, then append `rd.break`. Boot with the on-screen key (usually Ctrl+x). At the `switch_root` prompt the installed system is mounted read-only at `/sysroot`.

```sh
mount -o remount,rw /sysroot
chroot /sysroot
passwd root
touch /.autorelabel
exit
exit
```

The first `exit` leaves the chroot and the second resumes startup. The relabel runs once and reboots the guest; let it finish. Log in as root with the new password and confirm with `id` and `getenforce`.

## Why the relabel matters
`passwd` writes a new `/etc/shadow`. The early shell does not load the SELinux policy, so the new file can get the wrong label, and a system with a mislabeled shadow file can reject every login. `/.autorelabel` asks the next normal boot to restore default contexts across the filesystem.

## An alternative entry point
If the early shell lacks `chroot`, edit the `linux` line again: change `ro` to `rw`, remove `rhgb quiet` and append `init=/bin/bash`. The root filesystem is then already writable at `/`. Run `passwd root` and `touch /.autorelabel`, then `exec /sbin/init` to continue startup. Either way the edit applies to this boot only. Confirm afterwards with `cat /proc/cmdline` that neither argument remains.

A GRUB password, Secure Boot policy or an encrypted root volume adds its own prompt before you reach a shell. On the exam, read the task for the machine and the account it names.

lessons.title: Control who can connect and what they can reach
lessons.body:
Use the untimed pair as an approved client and server. On the server inspect `systemctl status sshd` and `ss -lnt`. If OpenSSH server is installed but inactive, enable it with `sudo systemctl enable --now sshd`. Use your own guest account for this exercise.

On the client run `install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh` and check that workshop_id and workshop_id.pub are unused. Generate a dedicated key with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/workshop_id` and supply a passphrase. Compare the server's console output from `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` with the ED25519 host fingerprint when accepting the first connection. If the guest policy requires a different algorithm, use a supported key such as RSA with at least 3072 bits and check the host fingerprint for the algorithm actually negotiated. If SSH password login for learner is allowed, copy the public key with `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id.pub learner@192.168.77.10`. Otherwise log in locally on the server as learner, create `~/.ssh` with mode 700 and append the single line from the client's **.pub** file to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Set that file to 600 and restore its default SELinux context with `restorecon -RFv ~/.ssh`. Only the public key is copied.

Run `ssh -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey learner@192.168.77.10 hostname`. The server must accept the key for this test to succeed. Your private key may still ask for its local passphrase. Then transfer your own note using `scp -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey notes.txt learner@192.168.77.10:notes.received`. Create `notes.txt` locally first. Compare `sha256sum` on the two files. For a failed login, check the account, file ownership, mode, and `sudo journalctl -b -u sshd` on the server.

## Test a firewall rule in two stores
On a workshop guest with active firewalld, inspect `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`. Identify the zone for the test interface and substitute its name for ZONE. For an unused demonstration TCP port, query `sudo firewall-cmd --zone=ZONE --query-port=18080/tcp` in runtime and with `--permanent`. If neither allows it, add it first at runtime with `--add-port=18080/tcp` and repeat both queries. Make it persistent with the same add command plus `--permanent`. Reload and verify both queries. Remove only your two practice rules when finished. Opening a firewall port permits traffic to reach a listener; verify listening separately with `ss -lnt`.

`sftp` offers an interactive session over the same connection, and `rsync -av -e ssh SOURCE learner@192.168.77.10:DEST` copies only what changed when rsync is installed on both ends.

lessons.title: Test a listener and its firewall rule separately
lessons.body:
A server can allow traffic to a port where nothing is listening. It can also have a perfectly healthy listener that is unreachable from the client. To distinguish those conditions, make a request from each side of the firewall and inspect the interface's active zone.

## Set up a temporary known service
Use the untimed **server**. Identify the interface carrying `192.168.77.10` with `ip -brief address` and find its zone with `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`. Record that exact zone as `zone=NAME` in your shell. Verify that TCP port 18082 is unused with `ss -ltn` and that neither runtime nor permanent policy has a specific rule for it. If an existing service or rule already uses it, choose another unused practice port throughout. In an isolated course pair, run:

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'evening roster\n' > "$work/index.html"
python3 -m http.server 18082 --bind 192.168.77.10 --directory "$work" >"$work/http.log" 2>&1 &
web=$!
ss -ltn 'sport = :18082'
curl -fsS http://192.168.77.10:18082/
```

Expect the server request to return the roster. From the **client** issue `curl --max-time 4 http://192.168.77.10:18082/`. Record the baseline. If traffic is already allowed by the zone's target or a broader rule, document it. A successful baseline cannot establish that your new rule opened a blocked path.

## Demonstrate runtime and persistent policy
On the server, run `sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$zone" --add-port=18082/tcp` and repeat the client request. Query both `sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$zone" --query-port=18082/tcp` and the same command with `--permanent`. Add the permanent rule only after checking the zone and result. Reload, query both stores again and repeat the remote request. Read the server log to identify which guest actually made the request.

## Isolate one failure
Stop your temporary server process with `kill "$web"`, keeping the firewall rule in place briefly. Try again from the client and inspect `ss` on the server. What single observation distinguishes a missing listener from the earlier firewall experiment?

**Check your work.** Report zone, listener and client response separately. Restore your baseline by removing only the practice port from each store to which you added it. Retest both queries. A firewall rule may survive boot while the short-lived Python process ends when its session ends.

lessons.title: Bring up a small web service and locate a failed request
lessons.body:
A branch office needs an internal status page. A successful request depends on several independent conditions. The web process must start, listen on the intended address, pass filesystem and SELinux checks, and receive traffic through the correct firewall zone. Test locally first, then from the client. Use your own disposable pair with a trusted RPM source.

## Get a known-good local result
On the server install httpd and curl if needed using DNF. On a fresh server create one file with `printf 'branch ready\n' | sudo tee /var/www/html/shift-status.txt`. Restore its normal policy label with `sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/shift-status.txt`. Run `sudo systemctl enable --now httpd` and `curl -i http://127.0.0.1/shift-status.txt`. Expect an HTTP 200 status and the marker. If startup fails, inspect `sudo apachectl configtest` and `sudo journalctl -b -u httpd`. A successful request for a different page does not establish access to this file.

With firewalld active, list `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`. Use the dedicated private zone from **Build your own client and server**. Verify the NAT interface belongs to another zone and its rules do not already allow HTTP. For this exercise set `zone=NAME` using that actual zone. If HTTP is not already allowed, apply `sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$zone" --add-service=http`. From the client run `curl -i --max-time 5 http://192.168.77.10/shift-status.txt`. Add the same service with `--permanent` when you intend this private service to survive a reload. Reload and repeat the client request. Record whether the rule was already present before changing anything.

**Interpret three outcomes.** A 404 means an HTTP server answered but the requested resource was not found. A 403 means HTTP answered but refused access; inspect path traversal, the server config, the journal and SELinux evidence. A timeout gives no HTTP status; check the route, address binding and firewall. In each case identify the first layer that already worked.

**Independent ticket.** Publish a second marker and request it by a lab hostname from the client. Save the status line, body and serving host. Reboot the server and repeat from the client. If you opened the rule solely for this exercise, remove only the HTTP service rule you added from both runtime and permanent configuration.

lessons.title: Diagnose access from the account that needs it
lessons.body:
An operator says a report is “permission denied” and asks for broader access to the entire server. First identify who performed the failing action, which object they attempted to access and whether they needed to read an existing file or replace it. Check ordinary permissions and directory traversal before investigating a service's SELinux domain.

## Reproduce a small failure
On the untimed client as learner, build a private directory you own. Leave the shell's working directory outside it so that the following test reflects path traversal by a new process.

```sh
work=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir "$work/reports"
printf 'morning roster\n' > "$work/reports/daily"
chmod 644 "$work/reports/daily"
chmod 600 "$work/reports"
id
namei -l "$work/reports/daily"
cat "$work/reports/daily"
```

The owner can read and write directory entries as permissions allow, but cannot traverse this directory without its execute bit. `cat` should fail for the ordinary account although the file's own mode allows reading. Repair just the missing permission with `chmod u+x "$work/reports"` and retry as the same learner. Collect `stat -c '%A %U:%G %n'` on both objects. A test performed solely as root would give misleading evidence about ordinary access.

## Apply the reasoning to a service
On the server, compare `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt` and `ps -eZ | grep httpd`. A process domain is the SELinux type of a running process. A file type labels the object. A service may be denied after the ordinary identity checks succeed. If httpd is stopped, there is no running httpd worker to inspect. In the following service lab, repeat this observation with the daemon running and test the actual URL.

## Write a repair note
Given a world-readable page under a private parent directory, predict the first ordinary failure for a service account. Given a correctly traversable document root containing a file moved from a home directory, name a label comparison that could explain a second failure. Decide which layer each repair addresses.

**Check your work.** Put the failing actor, operation, path, first failing observation, smallest correction and repeated test in your note. Keep the service under enforcing policy for the later web checks. A successful `cat` as learner is evidence for that account, while an HTTP response from the client demonstrates the service path.

lessons.title: Diagnose a denial while keeping access controls intact
lessons.body:
A web document is readable by ordinary file mode, yet a confined service cannot access it. Check identity, traversal and standard permissions, then examine SELinux. Use `getenforce`, `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, `ps -eZ` and `sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` when the audit tools are present. Compare an affected file's type with `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt`. The policy convention for read-only web content under the normal document root is `httpd_sys_content_t`.

In the untimed server, use `sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html` if needed. If the example.txt name is unused, create it with `sudo touch /var/www/html/example.txt`. Compare `ls -Z /var/www/html/example.txt` with `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt`. On this disposable file, run `sudo chcon --reference="$HOME" /var/www/html/example.txt`. Observe the changed type, then run `sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/example.txt` on the file you created. A file moved from another directory can retain its old label. A copy or rename is no substitute for checking the resulting context.

## Move the policy with the application
For an alternate document root on a guest with semanage, create `/srv/workshop-web` and a test file. Add the path rule `sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/workshop-web(/.*)?'`, then apply it with `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/workshop-web`. Check actual and expected labels. For a web service that needs a different listening port, inspect `semanage port -l` and, on an unused training port with no existing specific assignment, practice `sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 18081`. Verify the mapping and remove your new mapping with `sudo semanage port -d -p tcp 18081` when finished. To retire the alternate document-root rule, use `sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/workshop-web(/.*)?'` and `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/workshop-web`. Firewall policy and SELinux port labels are independent.

Inspect `getsebool httpd_can_network_connect` and `semanage boolean -l`. In a disposable guest where that capability is needed, record the current value, apply `sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on` and verify, then restore the original value. To observe enforcement modes on the untimed disposable guest only, record the current mode, compare `getenforce` after `sudo setenforce 0` and `sudo setenforce 1`, and finish in enforcing mode. On this already labeled guest, check that /etc/selinux/config sets SELINUX=enforcing. Reboot and confirm `getenforce` reports Enforcing. setenforce by itself changes the running kernel. A denial identifies a policy decision to investigate. For ordinary default permissions, compare newly created files and directories under `umask 027` in a subshell. Expect 640 and 750 from ordinary creation modes.

**Read a denial.** In a web AVC, find scontext (the process), tcontext (the object), tclass (what kind of object) and the requested permission in braces. For a read of a file with an unexpected type, compare the expected label with matchpathcon before changing policy. If a repair alters a label in place but restorecon reverses it, persist the intended path mapping with semanage fcontext and apply it. Confirm by serving the actual page under enforcement.

`umask` changes only the current shell. To keep a value for one user's future shells, add a line such as `umask 027` to that user's `~/.bashrc`. For all users' login shells, put it in a new script under `/etc/profile.d/` with a `.sh` name. Open a new login and run `umask` to verify.

lessons.title: Lab • Repair a web document label
lessons.body:
On the **server**, create the regular file `/var/www/html/erudior-status.txt` and give it the SELinux type for ordinary read-only web content, `httpd_sys_content_t`. Leave enforcement enabled. A short status line of your choice is sufficient.

Inspect the actual file type and context, the expected default context for this path, and the global enforcement mode. Avoid following a symlink to an unrelated file. If a relabel changes the type back, inspect the path's persistent policy mapping. Submit after the actual file and mode satisfy the task.

## Reason through a reported result
The document is 0644 and its expected context is httpd_sys_content_t, but ls -Z shows a home-directory type. What comparison will prove the repair?

**Check your reasoning.** Compare actual and expected types after applying the persistent label convention. Keep enforcement active and check the actual document on the next boot.

lessons.title: Lab • Serve web content on a custom port
lessons.body:
On the **server**, make `httpd` serve `/var/www/html` on TCP port 18080, running now and at boot. Allow the port through firewalld permanently and keep SELinux enforcing.

Three separate controls must agree. Add `Listen 18080` to the Apache configuration (`/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf` or a file in `/etc/httpd/conf.d/`). Label the port for the web server with `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 18080`; without the label, enforcing SELinux stops httpd from binding the port and `journalctl -u httpd` shows a permission error. Open the firewall with `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=18080/tcp` and `firewall-cmd --reload`. Then `systemctl enable --now httpd`.

Test with `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:18080/` on the server and `curl -I http://192.168.77.10:18080/` from the client. A 403 for an empty document root still proves the server answered. The grader checks the service, the listener, the firewall rule, enforcing mode and an HTTP answer, then repeats after a reboot.

lessons.title: Lab • Key-based SSH login between the machines
lessons.body:
Create the user `labssh` on the **server**. On the **client**, let the `learner` account log in to the server as `labssh` with an SSH key and no password prompt.

On the client as learner, create a key pair with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` (an empty passphrase lets the grader log in unattended). The server image may refuse password logins over SSH, so `ssh-copy-id` can fail. In that case copy the contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` from the client and, on the server console, append it to `/home/labssh/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The directory must be mode 700 and the file 600, both owned by labssh. Run `restorecon -Rv /home/labssh/.ssh` if you created them in an unusual way.

Test from the client with `ssh -o BatchMode=yes labssh@192.168.77.10 true; echo $?`. Zero means a key login worked without prompting. The grader runs the same kind of test as learner on the client, before and after the client reboots.

lessons.title: Rehearsal • Hand off a working file service
lessons.body:
A shift change is approaching. The client needs an operator and a way to find and consume the server's data. The server needs a private team workspace and a dependable startup service. Use the five task cards below as the acceptance criteria. This timed rehearsal starts with fresh machines. It does not inherit work from the individual labs.

Before opening a console, draw two columns headed Client and Server. Allocate 5 minutes to map the tasks, 30 to implement them and 15 to test as the affected user. Verify the lookup and mount from the client. Verify ownership and startup behavior on the server. Partition your checks so a failure in one area does not mask evidence in another. For example, test address routing independently of hostname lookup.

Each task is worth 10 points. After submission identify the first missing observation and return to the corresponding lab. Aim to earn all 50 points before moving on.

## Reason through a reported result
The client resolves the correct address, but an NFS marker comes from the root volume. The server’s team directory passes. Which task remains open?

**Check your reasoning.** The client mount still needs a working trigger. Keep the passing server evidence separate, then verify the mount by remote source and a fresh server marker.

On a manually prepared pair, use the same task cards as the brief. For each one, record what works before and after restarting the affected guest. Use the self-check to track your own practice.

lessons.title: Rehearsal • Bring a branch server back into service
lessons.body:
A branch office is returning to service. Its client needs a usable software source and a command an ordinary operator can execute. Its server needs memory backing, a tuning policy and a document with the correct security label. Work from the five task cards below. Use a fresh evidence sheet and solve them without consulting the earlier command examples.

Reserve the last 10 minutes for verification. Record the repository ID, two classifier boundary results, the active profile, usable swap and the file context. If a persistent setting looks right on disk, identify the live query that establishes it has actually taken effect. Submit once you have tested the operator's experience. Each task is worth 10 points.

Review both columns of the result. If everything passed before reboot but one item failed afterward, name the component responsible for restoring that item at boot. Repeat the corresponding focused lab before the final practical.

## Reason through a reported result
Both the tuning profile and the web label are correct after restart. A script passes for 9 but prints small for 10. Which change has the narrowest scope?

**Check your reasoning.** Repair the script boundary and rerun it as an ordinary client user. Keep the independently verified server states intact.

On a manually prepared pair, use the same task cards as the brief. For each one, record what works before and after restarting the affected guest. Use the self-check to track your own practice.

lessons.title: Independent practical: provision a branch archive
lessons.body:
A research branch is opening. Its manager requests a durable archive, a 06:15 receipt and a private status page. You receive a fresh disposable AlmaLinux 10 server, a client, a trusted RPM source and one new 2 GiB virtual disk on the server. Use your own pair or clones set aside for this exercise. The Erudior timed form uses separate machines. Budget 75 minutes for delivery and 30 for acceptance and repair. Use installed documentation. Keep the acceptance checks below folded away in your notes until you have attempted the work.

## Work order
1. Give the server an additional client-resolvable alias, archive.branch.test, on the private network. Create a local group called archivists and a regular user called mika on the server. Give mika membership in archivists and a password maximum age of 60 days.
2. On the **new disk only**, create one GPT partition, an LVM physical volume, a volume group called branchvg and a 512 MiB logical volume called records. Create an XFS filesystem and mount it persistently by UUID at /srv/records. Keep a marker file named origin with the value branch-one.
3. Give /srv/records to group archivists with mode 2770. As mika create a note. Increase the filesystem capacity by at least 192 MiB and retain both files. Verify a fresh group login can use the archive.
4. On the server install an executable called /usr/local/bin/branch-count. For each readable filename passed as an argument print its number of lines and its original name. If no argument is supplied, exit nonzero and write a diagnostic. Make it handle a filename containing spaces.
5. Configure a systemd calendar timer to record a journal entry tagged branch-receipt every day at 06:15 server time. The corresponding service must be safe to start manually. Enable the schedule and show evidence of one actual execution.
6. Serve /branch.txt over HTTP on the private interface with the text archive online. Keep SELinux enforcing. Open only the needed firewall service in the private zone. Test from the client using the new name.

## Acceptance record
Award one practice point for each numbered row that you can demonstrate. For persistent settings, require the same outcome after a normal server reboot. A script exercise is complete when the actual inputs produce the required output and exit statuses. Record a failed row and the observed result before you consult the worked lessons.

| Row | Independent observation |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | On the client, the alias resolves to the server's private address. A fresh server login for mika shows archivists. The aging report shows 60 days. |
| 2 | The mounted source's UUID matches the boot configuration. The marker came from XFS on branchvg/records. |
| 3 | Both files survive growth and reboot. A newly created file inherits archivists and the mounted directory has mode 2770. |
| 4 | Try a zero-line file, a two-line file with a space in its name, and no arguments. Inspect stdout, stderr and status separately. |
| 5 | Query the next scheduled activation. Start the paired service and find a new tagged event. Confirm the timer is waiting after reboot. |
| 6 | From the client, request the named host and exact resource. Capture HTTP 200 and the marker together. Check enforcement on the server. Identify the private interface’s zone and check the HTTP rule there in runtime and permanent configuration. Confirm the NAT zone does not already grant HTTP access. |

**Debrief.** If the marker disappeared, compare the filesystem serving the path before and after reboot. If a file has the wrong group, inspect the mounted directory and a newly created child. If the service works locally, test its private address, then the client's lookup and the firewall. Repeat any failed row on a fresh snapshot with new names. This is a self-scored practical; the next lesson records a separate machine-graded result in the desktop app.

lessons.title: Final • RHCSA practice exam for RHEL 10
lessons.body:
You have a new client, a new server and three hours. Read the ten tasks in the exam panel. Use the named machine for each and decide your own order. Both lab machines must identify as AlmaLinux 10.
